notes:
MAJOR UPDATE 2026-05-19 from wyrd-kz2b.25 — 'what LLMs can't do' positioning paragraph (draft, ~230 words, defensible):

> Recent evaluation work documents structural limits of LLMs on linguistic tasks that require explicit phonological or rule-based reasoning. Kallini et al. (2024) show that GPT-2 trained on synthetic 'impossible languages' learns these patterns less efficiently than natural English, supporting a continuum on which natural-language patterns sit at one end and structurally incoherent patterns at the other. Suvarna et al. (2024) document gaps of 17% (rhyme generation) and 45% (syllable counting) between leading LLMs and humans on phonological diagnostic tasks, and identify subword (BPE) tokenization as a root cause: phonological structure is destroyed at the input-encoding stage. Beguš, Dąbkowski, and Rhodes (2025) probe LLMs' ability to produce explicit linguistic analyses on novel test sets and find that even the strongest evaluated model (OpenAI o1) achieves only 63% accuracy on identifying phonological rule environments in SPE notation; the three non-reasoning models tested score below 14%. These results converge on a structural rather than merely-capability gap: LLM phonological representations are recoverable from orthography only imperfectly, and the production of explicit rule formalizations is unreliable. Wyrd's contribution is orthogonal to this line of work: its rule-based architecture encodes phonological structure explicitly at the morpheme level, with SPE-style derivations produced as a side effect of generation rather than as an inference task.

HONEST CAVEAT (per .26 lesson): avoid 'LLMs cannot do phonology' — they CAN do it partially. Honest framing is 'structural limits' with specific numbers.

EVALUATION METHODOLOGY BORROWS from this cluster: novel test sets specifically constructed to defeat memorization; multi-seed; multiple human graders (Beguš: 3); logistic mixed-effects regression for analysis.

title: Add tense-vs-lax vowel distinction to phonological-vector schema
description: wyrd-2166 surfaced: Whissell 2000's vowel ratings are non-monotonic in height (/iː/ Gentle, /ɪ/ Harsh; /ɔ/ Gentle, /uː/ Harsh) — tense/lax matters more than front/back. The current 14 PhonologicalFeatureName dimensions don't capture this. Schema change: add vowel_tenseness dimension or split existing vowel features by tenseness. Coordinates with wyrd-kq7w.1 corpus enrichment. Source: Whissell 1999 PMS 89:19-48; restated 2017 p. 3.

title: Split soft_consonants dimension: /l m n/ vs /r/ (Whissell asymmetry)
description: wyrd-2166 surfaced: Whissell 2000 rates /l m n/ as firmly Gentle but /r/ as firmly Harsh ('l as sweet, r as tough', 2017 p. 3). The current PhonologicalFeatureName 'soft_consonants' dimension lumps them, so /r/-heavy lemmas score high on softness when they should read the opposite. Schema change: split into liquid_l_m_n (or finer per-place features) and rhotic_r. Requires coordinating with wyrd-kq7w.1 (phonological-vector corpus enrichment) so existing per-lemma vectors get the new dimensions. Sources: Fort/Martin/Peperkamp 2015; Whissell 1999/2000/2017; Sidhu & Pexman 2024.

title: Research: scholarly grounding for register-effect catalog weights
description:
The v1 register_effects.yaml catalog (shipped wyrd-kq7w.2 / PR #235) hand-tuned weights for 12 register effects (grim, harsh, pastoral, devotional, mortuary + noble, mystical, melodic, sinister, ancient, exotic, martial) based on intuition + faithfulness to the legacy MOODS dict. The weights are 'reasonable' but unvalidated against any phonaesthetics literature, empirical sound-symbolism studies, or cross-cultural register research.

This ticket scopes the scholarly research pass that would let us defend each register's weight set + identify which dimensions are under- or over-weighted relative to the literature.

PRIMARY SOURCES TO REVIEW:
- Hinton, Nichols, Ohala (eds.) 1994 'Sound Symbolism' (Cambridge UP). The foundational compilation; covers iconic / synesthetic / conventional sound-symbolism across languages. Pull chapters relevant to: cluster density (harshness perception), final fortition / coda voicing (firmness), vowel-final bias (softness/openness), palatalization (intimacy/diminutive vs distance), retroflexion (exoticism in non-retroflex languages).
- Köhler 1929 / Maluma-Takete (later 'bouba-kiki'). Round vs spiky shape perception correlated with vowel backness + consonant continuancy. Bears on pastoral/harsh + melodic/sinister.
- Ohala 'frequency code' (1984, 1994 in the Sound Symbolism volume). Pitch + size + dominance signaling. Bears on noble (low formants → grand) vs mystical (high formants → ethereal).
- Whissell phonemic-emotion studies (Whissell 1999, 2003, 2011). Empirical mapping of individual phonemes to emotion ratings (pleasantness, activity, arousal). Direct input for which phonemes to weight + 1 vs -1 on which register.
- Lockwood, Dingemanse, Hagoort 2016+ on ideophones / iconicity universality. Cross-cultural validation of the western-bias of the above.
- Crystal 1995 'The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the English Language' for established 'mellifluous' / 'harsh' phonotactic classifications already named in the linguistic tradition.

PRIMARY OUTPUTS:
- For each of the 12 v1 register effects, document the phonological-dimension weights with citations to the sources above. Either confirm the v1 weight or propose an adjusted weight with rationale.
- Identify new register effects the literature suggests we should add. Candidates likely include 'monumental' (extra-long syllables + low-formant vowels), 'whimsical' (high-vowel + diminutive palatalization), 'archaic-celtic' (vs the current generic ancient which is monolingual-substrate-ambiguous), 'liturgical' (vs devotional — open syllables + Latin-shaped polysyllables).
- Identify the 14 PhonologicalFeatureName dimensions that turn out to be under-represented or genuinely ambiguous and propose schema-level refinements (would require coordinating with the Phase A corpus-vector work wyrd-kq7w.1).
- Decide whether semantic_tags weights need calibration. The v1 catalog uses tag weights in [0.2, 0.8] based on rough intuition; an empirical pass would look at meaning-DB tag co-occurrence rates and propose calibrated weights.

DELIVERABLES (in order):
1. New doc wyrd/generators/kenning/REGISTERS.md (or sections in DECISIONS.md) with per-register scholarly grounding + per-weight citation.
2. Catalog update — register_effects.yaml weights adjusted per the research; the existing tests will catch any [-1, +1] / dimension-name violations automatically.
3. Optional follow-up tickets for new register effects + new phonological dimensions.

OUT OF SCOPE:
- Per-language phonological inventory studies (those are the wyrd-v2gm fantasy-language epic territory).
- The mood→register migration acceptance test (depends on wyrd-kq7w.1 + wyrd-kq7w.3 landing first).
- Cross-cultural validation of register effect names themselves (a separate research pass).

PRIORITY: P3 — the v1 catalog is shippable as-is for early-iteration generator work; scholarly grounding becomes more valuable once the kenning pipeline is actively producing user-facing names that depend on register choices. Open the research when wyrd-ecjp.4 (vector scoring runtime) lands and we have real outputs to validate against.
notes: Surfaced from kq7w.2 review-loop discussion 2026-05-18. The v1 weights are intentional hand-tuned defaults; scholarly grounding is the path from 'reasonable defaults' to 'defensible architecture decision'.

title: Use Briggs PN attested-form variants to enrich mine-llm prompting + post-extraction validation
description:
Architectural follow-on to wyrd-uzoh's expanded scope (personal_name_attested_forms artifact). Briggs gives us per-PN orthographic variant sets across many toponyms (e.g. Ēadwulf → Eadulf-, Edulues-, Adl-, Edl-, Eden-, Adolf-, Adel-, Eadulfing-). This data should improve mine-llm (Pipeline 2 etymology extraction) in two distinct ways:

1. PROMPT ENRICHMENT (proactive). When mine-llm runs against a dictionary entry whose toponym has a Briggs attribution, the prompt should include the PN's known attested-form set as context: 'This toponym is Briggs-attributed to PN Ēadwulf, whose attested historical forms include Eadulf-, Edulues-, Adl-, Edl-, Eden-, Adolf-, Adel-. Identify the rest of the elements after stripping the PN.' This collapses the open-set 'what PN is this' guess into a closed-set 'verify and parse the residual' task. Expected effect: meaningful precision lift on the PN-side of the extraction for Briggs-covered toponyms.

2. POST-EXTRACTION VALIDATION (reactive). After mine-llm produces an etymology decomposition, compare against Briggs's authoritative answer:
   - If Briggs attributes the toponym to PN X and LLM extracted PN Y, flag the divergence
   - If Briggs has no PN attribution but LLM extracted a PN element, that's a hypothesis the EPNS scholars didn't endorse (could be LLM hallucination OR a genuine candidate they missed — operator review case)
   - If both agree, mark high-confidence consensus (Briggs + LLM both saying PN=Eadwulf is stronger than either alone)

Fix scope:

a. Extend mine-llm's per-entry prompt template to optionally include a 'briggs_context' section when the toponym has a Briggs attribution. Pull the (PN_headform, attested_form_variants) from the personal_name_attested_forms table at prompt-build time.

b. Add a flag to mine-llm: '--use-briggs-context BOOL' (default True when Briggs data is available, easy to disable for A/B testing).

c. Post-extraction validation step: new CLI subcommand 'wyrd kenning lexicon validate-llm-etymology-vs-briggs' that runs the comparison and produces a report:
   - LLM-Briggs agreement rate per source
   - Per-source LLM-only PN hypotheses (operator review candidates)
   - Per-source Briggs-only PN attributions the LLM missed (extractor weakness signals)

d. (Bonus, possibly out of scope) Apply Briggs variant matching to the staged-cascade pipeline too — when the prose-extractor sees a toponym that contains a known attested-form variant ('Eaduluesbreche' contains 'Eadulu-'), surface the PN attribution metadata. The staged pipeline doesn't do etymology, but it could ENRICH mentions with 'this toponym contains PN-variant X (from Briggs)' annotations.

A/B measurement plan:

- Pick a Briggs-rich county (e.g. Yorkshire NRY with EPNS data we already have)
- Run mine-llm WITHOUT briggs_context on a random 50-entry sample
- Run mine-llm WITH briggs_context on the same 50 entries
- Compare extraction quality: PN agreement with Briggs, element-position correctness, element-language tag correctness
- Lift expected: 10-25%% precision on the PN-side, smaller lift on the rest of the etymology

Out of scope:
- Briggs ingester itself (wyrd-uzoh) — prerequisite
- Deterministic decomposer (wyrd-1zx9) — separate downstream consumer of Briggs
- Generator-side use of variant sets — separate ticket

This is a 'quality multiplier' ticket — same mine-llm pipeline, better data flowing through it. Could potentially halve the LLM error rate on Briggs-covered toponyms.

title: Programmatic toponym decomposer using Briggs PN attribution + Mawer 1924 element vocabulary
description:
Architectural follow-on to wyrd-uzoh (Briggs personal-names index ingestion). Once the Briggs personal-name → toponym attribution is in the lexicon, we can do mechanical structural parsing of any toponym Briggs covers — no LLM needed for that subset.

The insight: toponym decomposition is hard for an LLM because the personal-name half is open-set (thousands of attested OE/ON/ME personal names). Briggs supplies that half authoritatively (EPNS-scholar-vetted). Mawer 1924 'The Chief Elements Used in English Place-Names' (already ingested in our corpus) supplies the closed-set half — the toponym-forming morpheme vocabulary, maybe 100-150 productive elements covering both settlement (tūn, hām, wīc, worð, byrig, cot) and topographic (dūn, hyll, denu, dæl, cumb, ford, ēa, brōc, lēah, wudu, ēg, mōr, gara, æcer, …) compounds, plus the genitive/folk connector morphemes (-es-, -s, -inga-).

Given a toponym Briggs covers, the parse becomes deterministic:

1. Strip the personal-name root from the toponym form (Briggs gives us PN = Ēadwulf for Adlington (Ch))
2. Longest-suffix match the residual against Mawer's element table (-lington → -ing- + -tūn)
3. Emit a fully structured parse: [PN_Ēadwulf, OE] + [-inga-, gen pl] + [tūn, OE settlement]

For non-settlement compounds: Eden's Hill (Gl), Eduluesbreche (Brk = brēc), Eadulfing garan (Gl = gara), Eadulfi clausum (Wo) — same algorithm; the suffix-match step just hits a topographic element instead of a settlement element.

Value:

1. For the ~15-25%% of English toponyms covered by Briggs, replace LLM etymology mining with deterministic decomposition. EPNS-scholar quality, zero LLM cost, zero hallucination on those rows.
2. Quality oracle for LLM proposals: when gemma4/haiku/gemini propose an etymology for a Briggs-covered toponym, compare against the deterministic parse. Divergences are quality signals (especially LLMs missing the -inga- folk-genitive, which is common).
3. Kenning generator unlocks topographic-feature templates (<PN>'s hill, <PN>'s dale, <PN>'s ford) alongside the existing settlement templates (<PN>'s tūn, <PN>'s hām). The current generator is settlement-biased because that's what the multi-extractor consensus is best at.

Fix scope:

1. Element-vocabulary loader: parse mawer_1924_chief_elements (already in lexicon) into a structured table — for each element, capture (form, language, semantic_category, attested_variant_spellings, productive_period). Categories: settlement / topographic-landform / topographic-water / topographic-flora / topographic-parcel / connector / road-structure.

2. Personal-name-stripper: given a toponym form + a known PN root from Briggs, strip the PN (with sound-change tolerance — Ēadwulf → 'Ad-', 'Ed-', 'Eden-', 'Edul-', 'Edl-', etc. depending on the local OE→ME→ModE sound development). May need a small phonological-tolerance table per personal-name → orthographic-variant for the well-attested name patterns Briggs lists.

3. Element-matcher: longest-suffix match the stripped residual against the element-vocabulary table. Handle the connector morphemes (-inga-, -es-) as productive prefixes on the element side. Return the full decomposition or 'no match' for residuals that don't parse.

4. Lexicon writes: emit deterministic_decomposition rows tagged source_doc='briggs+mawer_decomposer' for every Briggs-covered toponym. Mark as 'canonical' equivalent to the multi-extractor-consensus canonical (same downstream consumers).

5. Quality-oracle CLI: 'wyrd kenning lexicon validate-llm-etymology' — for each toponym with both a deterministic decomposition AND LLM-proposed etymons, surface mismatches as a report. Flag systematic LLM errors (missing -inga-, wrong element family, etc.) for prompt tuning.

6. (Generator-side, separate ticket) Templates that consume the topographic + settlement element families directly: <PN>'s <element-family> with element-family chosen by request narrative.

Out of scope of this ticket:

- The Briggs ingestion itself (wyrd-uzoh) — prerequisite.
- Generator-side template wiring — separate consumer ticket.
- Sound-change rule generalization (we use a small per-name variant table for v1; full OE→ModE phonological rules are wyrd-v2gm.3.2 territory).
- Toponyms NOT covered by Briggs — these still go through the LLM etymology pipeline; the decomposer is opportunistic, not exhaustive.

Calibration target: Bedlington (toponym #151 in our lexicon, the existing multi-extractor-consensus calibration case). Briggs presumably has it as PN bedeling + tūn (or similar). Verify the deterministic decomposer produces the same parse the multi-extractor consensus already landed on for this row. If yes, the algorithm is ready for broader application; if not, the residual disagreement is a useful pinning case.

Pairs with: wyrd-uzoh (Briggs ingest, prerequisite), kenning generator template work, the canonical etymology pipeline (wyrd-08qv shipped — PR #222).

title: Ingest Briggs EPNS personal-names index → toponym ↔ personal-name relation
description:
Briggs 2024 "An Index to Personal Names in English Place-Names" (3rd rev. edn, EPNS Supplementary Series 2) is a downloadable EPNS reference at https://www.nottingham.ac.uk/research/groups/epns/documents/briggs-an-index-to-personal-names-in-english-place-names-3rd-edn.pdf. It compiles the personal-name → toponym mapping across the full EPNS corpus (Cameron's Lincolnshire, Gelling's Shropshire, Mills's Dorset, Reaney's Cambridgeshire, Cox's Leicestershire, etc.) — county volumes we mostly can't access otherwise.

Shape: per personal name, a list of toponyms containing that name with two-letter county codes (Ch, Li, Sa, Wo, ...) plus citation refs (PASE#, DLV, ASCh#). Different shape from our toponym etymology dictionaries — separate ingester needed.

The value proposition is three-fold:

1. Anti-hallucination ground truth on personal-name etymons. When the LLM extracts a toponym and proposes a personal-name element (e.g. Adlington → Eadwulf), we can verify the EPNS-scholar-vetted answer matches. Currently we have no check on the personal-name portion of LLM-proposed etymons.

2. Vetted personal-name pool for the kenning generator's 'Xs-ham / Xs-ton / Xs-ingham' patterns. Briggs is the curated list of personal names that historically actually appeared in English toponyms — the exact pool the generator should be drawing from rather than ad-hoc lexicon scraping.

3. Geographic distribution signal. Some personal names appear in 10+ counties (productive); others single-occurrence. Useful for regional plausibility judgments at generation time.

Estimated scale: ~5-15k personal-name headforms × 1-50+ toponym attestations each = 50-200k (personal_name, toponym, county) triples.

Copyright posture: Briggs's notice is strict EPNS-standard but the underlying facts (Eadwulf appears in Adlington) draw from the EPNS county volumes — those facts aren't copyrightable post-Feist. Use pattern matches our existing NC-licensed sources: ingest facts as a citation-bearing relation in the lexicon DB; don't ship the index itself in the bundle; computational derivatives flow into bundle as usual.

Staged at /tmp/wyrd-source-staging/briggs_2024_personal_names_index.txt (741K, pdftotext output of the EPNS-distributed PDF).

Fix scope:
1. New ingester module: wyrd/generators/kenning/briggs_personal_names_ingester.py.
2. County-code mapping table: parse the 'Coverage' section (head of the PDF) which lists each two-letter code with its full county name (Bd=Bedfordshire, Brk=Berkshire, Bk=Buckinghamshire, Ca=Cambridgeshire, Ch=Cheshire, Cu=Cumberland, Db=Derbyshire, D=Devon, Do=Dorset, Du=County Durham, Ess=Essex, Gl=Gloucestershire, Ha=Hampshire, He=Herefordshire, Hrt=Hertfordshire, ...). Codify as a module-level constant after extracting; spot-check against the EPNS volume titles.
3. Index parser: stream the index section (page 19+ in PDF / line 797+ in extracted .txt). Each entry leads with a personal-name headform (often with diacritics — Ēadwulf, Æthelric, etc.). Each entry's body contains source-citation refs (PASE#, DLV, ASCh#) interleaved with toponym attestations of the form 'Toponym (CC)' or 'Toponym CC' or with date qualifiers ('Adlington (1278)' / 'Adelwesdenn in Rolvenden (KW)'). Parse carefully — the two-column PDF→text flattening interleaves entries across columns; need to detect headform-start lines vs continuation lines.
4. Schema: new table 'toponym_personal_name_attestations' with columns (toponym_form, personal_name_headform, personal_name_language_hint, county_code, county_canonical, source_doc='briggs_2024_personal_names_index', source_citation, page_number). Or augment toponym_etymology with a 'personal_name_headform' nullable column and a separate facts table. Decide schema-side in the design step.
5. Join to existing toponym table by (form, region_hint=county_canonical). Many Briggs toponyms will already exist in our lexicon with attestations from the gap-region sources we're queuing up; this is a many-to-many join that materially enriches both sides.
6. CLI subcommand: 'wyrd kenning lexicon ingest-briggs-personal-names'. Idempotent (skip if row exists by source_doc + headform + toponym + county); progress reporting per the workspace convention.
7. (Anti-hallucination check — out-of-scope of this ticket; file as follow-up) Add a validator step to toponym_mention_extractor that consults this relation when the LLM proposes a personal-name etymon, flagging mismatch as a quality signal.

Out of scope:
- The anti-hallucination wiring (item 7) — that's a separate ingestion-consumer ticket.
- Generator-side use of the vetted personal-name pool (the wyrd-v2gm / wyrd-ecjp fantasy-language epics) — separate downstream consumer work.
- Manual review / verification pass — the data is EPNS-scholar-vetted; trust the source.

Related work:
- Pairs with the gap-source mining work (Bannister Cornish, Sedgefield Cumbria, Hill Somerset, Horsley Kent, Warwickshire EPNS, etc.) — once both have ingested, the join surface is large.
- The wyrd-ialp wave-2 corpus expansion epic is the natural parent epic.
notes:
Scope clarification (2026-05-18): the ingester MUST emit two artifacts, not one. Per follow-up architectural discussion:

1. (personal_name, toponym, county) triples — the primary mapping (original scope).

2. (personal_name_headform, attested_orthographic_variant, source_toponym, region) — the PN's surface-form variants extracted from each toponym entry. Briggs per-PN entries naturally contain this data already (a single Ēadwulf entry gives us Eadulf-, Edulues-, Adl-, Edl-, Eden-, Adolf-, Adel- variants from its toponym attestations). Exposing this as a first-class output unlocks multiple downstream consumers:

   - Pipeline 2 (mine-llm) prompt enrichment — the LLM can be TOLD the canonical PN when processing a Briggs-covered toponym, removing the open-set guess of "what PN is in this name"
   - Surface-form recognition outside dictionary sources — when staged-cascade prose-extractor sees "Eaduluesbreche" in random prose, lookup against the variant set deterministically resolves the PN
   - Sound-change empirical derivation — feeds the OE→ME→EModE→ModE phonological evolution work for wyrd-v2gm.3.x recipient-era phonology schemas
   - Period-forms work (wyrd-m92v) — attestation chains per PN are directly the input wyrd-m92v needs

Schema for the second artifact: a new table 'personal_name_attested_forms' with columns (pn_headform, pn_language, attested_form, source_toponym, source_toponym_county, source_doc='briggs_2024_personal_names_index'). Foreign keys to the (PN, toponym, county) primary table on pn_headform.

Staging path update (2026-05-18): briggs_2024_personal_names_index.txt + .pdf moved from /tmp/wyrd-source-staging/ to ~/521Studios/wyrd-source-staging/ (full path: /home/devon/521Studios/wyrd-source-staging/briggs_2024_personal_names_index.{txt,pdf}). /tmp is wiped on reboot; staging now persists. Replace any references to the /tmp path in the description.
close_reason: Shipped via PR #276 (merge commit 76f2ef1). Parser + schema + CLI for Briggs EPNS personal-names index. 10,929 entries → 8,881 personal_name rows + 15,021 attestation rows. 2 review rounds, all Gemini comments resolved, CI green. Tests + silent-skip counters + complexity refactor tracked in expanded wyrd-jac1.

title: Canonical toponym-etymology promotion via multi-extractor consensus
description:
Today: each LLM pass over a source produces a toponym_etymology row tagged with extracted_by:<provider:model>. Bedlington (toponym#151) has 3 rows from qwen3.5:9b + claude-haiku-4-5 + gemini-2.5-flash, all with confidence='high', all decomposing to bedeling(a) + tūn. They all agree but nothing marks one as canonical, and downstream consumers (proportions, generation) have to pick.

Gap: there's no 'toponym_etymology_canonical' equivalent of the etymon_canonical / etymon_consensus tables (which exist at the etymon level with 2.3M / 2.2M rows respectively).

User insight 2026-05-17: 'if this one is canonical, we don't need to test other variants against it.' i.e. once 2+ extractors agree, the answer is settled. Stop re-extracting, stop comparing.

WORKFLOW:
1. Cluster toponym_etymology rows for the same toponym_id by (element-set, ordinals, languages). Identical clusters = agreement.
2. Promote: when a cluster has >=2 extractor witnesses (different extracted_by tags), mark canonical (new column or sibling table).
3. Disagreement queue: clusters with single witnesses, or multiple clusters per toponym, go to operator-review.
4. Downstream consumers read canonical-only by default.
5. Future LLM re-extraction passes can short-circuit canonical toponyms — saves cost on re-mining settled answers.

ACCEPTANCE:
- A new column or table marking canonical toponym_etymology rows
- A CLI command (e.g. extend rando-port-readiness or new canonicalize-toponym-etymology) that computes consensus + marks canonical in one transaction
- Audit trail JSONL events (matches the existing curation event pattern)
- A 'show canonical etymology for toponym X' query path consumed by wyrd-m92v's proportions work
- Future LLM extraction passes skip toponyms with canonical etymology (cost optimization)

RELATED:
- wyrd-m92v (proportions/period-forms work) is the primary downstream consumer
- Same pattern as etymon_canonical / etymon_consensus but one layer up
- The 'single-attestation promotes' rule for wyrd-4453 is the rando layer's version of this

PRIORITY: P3 — downstream of corpus mining + ingest, but unblocks proportions consumer.
notes: PR #222 opened 2026-05-17. Schema migration + library + CLI + 36 tests. Smoke-verified end-to-end against live DB: Bedlington (toponym#151) — qwen+gemini agree on 'bedeling + tun' (canonical, 2 witnesses), haiku's richer 'bedeling + tun + bedel' is the runner-up. Awaiting review loop.
close_reason: Merged to main via PR #222 (squash) 2026-05-18. 3-round review loop + R3 verification with 14-agent fanout per round. Final state: canonicalize-toponym-etymology CLI command + library with multi-extractor consensus promotion. Bedlington (toponym#151) test pin: qwen+gemini agree on bedeling+tun (canonical), haiku's richer bedeling+tun+bedel is runner-up. 51 tests pinning: anonymous-witness semantics (0 witnesses), empty-elements early detection, JSON-encoded cluster keys (collision-resistant), N+1 → bulk-load + executemany, frozen CanonicalDecision, total_changes rowcount, _plans_from_decisions correctness (re-derives from current DB), _RowUpdate NamedTuple. Downstream consumers (wyrd-m92v proportions, wyrd-4453 rando retirement) can now read toponym_etymology_canonical view.

title: Ground proportions/period-forms work in corpus attestation chains (not just phonological projection)
description:
The corpus mining + ingest pipeline (wyrd-x82p) produces rich attestation chains: e.g. toponym#151 (Bedlington) has 8 distinct attested spellings across 1050-1507, era-bucketable from the date_year on each attestation row.

The existing project-period-forms (wyrd-unuo Phase 3.3) computes per-era reflexes via phonological rules. With attestation chains available, we can:

1. GROUND the projected forms against attested ones — if project-period-forms says 'Bedlington at 1100 should be Bedlingtun' and the attestations say 'Bedlingtun and Bethlingtun were both attested in 1085-1104', we have empirical confirmation + an alternate variant the projection didn't surface.

2. REPLACE projection with attested-set sampling where attestations exist — for the proportions / period-appropriate generation work, sample from the attested variant set for an era rather than projecting one canonical form from rules.

3. EXTEND lemma data — store per-era attested variants on the lemma itself so downstream consumers (proportions, generation, search) can query 'all attested forms of toponym#151 in the 12th century' without re-joining to toponym_attestation each time.

User note 2026-05-17: 'our existing approach wouldn't match in here, but we can use this to add variants to the known lemma for the different time spans' — i.e., the current matcher doesn't recognize Bedlingtun as a variant of Bedlington, but the attestation data tells us it IS.

ACCEPTANCE:
- A way to read all attested forms for a (toponym_id, era_bucket) pair (era buckets per the project-period-forms convention — pre-Conquest, Norman, late-medieval, etc.)
- The proportions / generation pipeline can consume this as an empirically-grounded alternative to the phonological projection
- Documentation of the trade-off: attested-set is sparse (only forms scholars cited) but real; projection is dense (every era covered) but reconstructive. Pick per-use-case.

PRE-REQS:
- wyrd-srd2 staged-cascade corpus mining complete enough to have broad per-source attestation coverage
- ingest-toponym-mentions + commit-toponym-candidates landed for those mining outputs (so attestations live in the DB, not just JSONL)
- wyrd-4453 rando retirement workflow can run in parallel — independent

PRIORITY: P3 — downstream of corpus mining + rando retirement, useful but not blocking either.

title: Consider delta-returning ValidationCounters from _run_hallucination_rescue + extract_toponym_mentions_from_chunk together
description:
Gemini wyrd-z8mq R7 MEDIUM + type-design-analyzer R7: _run_hallucination_rescue mutates primary_counters in-place rather than returning a delta. Architectural-cleanliness concern, not a bug — the mutation is correct, tested, idiomatic for this file (matches extract_toponym_mentions_from_chunk's pattern).

Refactoring just _run_hallucination_rescue alone would make the file LESS consistent (one delta-return, one mutation). The right scope is to consider both helpers together, ideally as part of the wyrd-kg22 orchestrator extraction work which already touches that area.

Specifics:
- extract_toponym_mentions_from_chunk(client, chunk, counters=...) → counters mutated in place
- _run_hallucination_rescue(..., primary_counters, ...) → primary_counters mutated in place

A delta-return shape would be: helper returns (mentions, rescue_counters, ok) and caller decides whether to fold rescue_counters into the chunk's accumulator. Cleaner separation of concerns but more verbose at call sites and a bigger refactor across both helpers.

Defer to whenever wyrd-kg22's orchestrator extraction lands. If that refactor happens, do this in the same PR for consistency.

title: Extract parse_transport_json helper for client envelope+inner JSON parses (rule-of-N satisfied)
description:
code-simplifier round-5 follow-up on wyrd-pe4g (PR #218). After the round-4 envelope wraps and the round-5 decode wraps, every chat_json in the kenning extractor stack uses the same try/except JSONDecodeError → RuntimeError pattern in 6 places (3 inner content parses + 3 outer envelope parses). The rule-of-N (4+ instances) is now satisfied.

The 6-line comment block on each new wrap is verbatim identical and asserts a CROSS-MODULE invariant — the _PROGRAMMER_ERROR_EXCEPTIONS carve-out it references lives in toponym_mention_extractor.py, not in the client files. The whole R3→R4 regression cycle happened because a maintainer didn't see that contract from inside one of these files. Three copies of a non-local invariant comment is exactly the kind of duplication that drifts.

Recommended extraction site: a parse_transport_json(payload, *, provider, kind) helper in llm_extractor.py (already a shared import target for anthropic_extractor.py and gemini_extractor.py). Collapses all 6 call sites to one line and centralizes the wyrd-pe4g invariant in one docstring.

Counter-argument (acknowledged): locality — per-provider error string is greppable, failure obvious inline, stack frame depth shorter. Trade-off; the maintainer who picks this up can weigh it.

Scope: the 6 wraps + their comment blocks. Out of scope: the dispatch-time guard, the schema_dialect ClassVar, the _PROGRAMMER_ERROR_EXCEPTIONS tuple (those stay where they are).

These are pre-existing wraps but currently have no transport-level test pin — only the new outer-envelope (R4) + decode (R5) paths got dedicated tests. The helper extraction is the natural place to add the missing 3 tests since they exercise the same helper. pr-test-analyzer R6 self-framed as 'not blocking', best paired with this issue's work.

title: EPIC: narrative-driven scenario translation (UX layer on top of vector machinery)
description:
Natural-language history descriptions translated via LLM into composed request vectors + scenario-pack subset admissions. Makes the vector machinery (wyrd-kq7w + the planned vector-driven generator epic + wyrd-v2gm scenario packs) accessible to GMs who think in narrative, not in linguistic vectors.

## The UX

User types a one-line narrative about the town's history:
- 'raided by horsemen in the 9th century'
- 'settled by sea-traders during the iron age'
- 'ancient ruins reclaimed by druids'
- 'sacked by an Eastern khanate then rebuilt as a trading post'

System emits a composed request specification covering era, register vector, and scenario-pack admissions with tag-filtered lemma subsets.

## Granularity insight (load-bearing)

Per-lemma register vectors (wyrd-kq7w.1) mean scenario packs aren't admitted whole-or-not. A scenario pack with N lemmas is a LEXICON; the narrative determines which subset to draw from via tag-filter + vector-distance. Same pack, different generative behavior per narrative.

Example: Mongol/Turkic scenario pack (~200 lemmas):
- 'raided by horsemen' -> subset tagged {military, equestrian, nomadic} at weight 0.4
- 'established a khanate' -> subset tagged {administrative, hierarchy, settlement} at weight 0.6
- 'plague swept the coast' -> subset tagged {death, disease, foreign-quality} at weight 0.2

## What's already in place

Most pieces exist or are planned in upstream epics:
- Per-lemma register vectors (wyrd-kq7w.1)
- Register-effect catalog (wyrd-kq7w.2)
- Scenario-pack lemmas with vectors (wyrd-v2gm)
- Vector-driven gating + scoring (planned epic in flight)
- LLM-grounded prompts (project already uses Gemini Flash extensively)

Narrative-translator is LLM glue on top.

## Phases

1. Schema: narrative-spec input format + derived-request-vector output format
2. Narrative-template library (curated mappings for common GM-trope situations: 'raided by X', 'settled by Y', 'haunted by Z', etc.) -- LLM prompt-grounding source
3. LLM-translator implementation: Gemini Flash with grounding in register-effect catalog + scenario-pack metadata + narrative-template library
4. CLI flag: 'wyrd kenning generate english --narrative "raided by horsemen 9c"'
5. SPA UX: narrative input box + rendered request-vector preview + generated names + edit/refine loop
6. Validation: spot-check that semantically-equivalent narratives produce equivalent name distributions; surprising or off-target outputs feed prompt iteration

## Why this matters

This is the **headline demo** of the whole system. 'Type your town's history; get plausibly-shaped names' is dramatically more compelling than 'compose a register-effect vector'. The vector machinery is the engine; the narrative-translator is the steering wheel.

Estimated 3-4 weeks: schema + LLM prompt + narrative-template library + CLI + SPA UX.

## Dependencies

Hard dep on:
- wyrd-kq7w.1 (per-lemma vectors)
- wyrd-kq7w.2 (register-effect catalog)
- TBD-filed vector-driven generator epic (vector-scoring runtime)
- wyrd-v2gm.6 (Neo-Khuzdul scenario-pack pilot to validate against)

Empirical loan-adaptation profile capturing Mon-Khmer + Tai-Kadai + Sino-Tibetan contact patterns in mainland SE Asia. Distinct from East Asian (Chinese/Japanese/Korean) which D11 deliberately excludes — focus here is on the substrate-and-loan patterns in Burma/Thailand/Cambodia/Vietnam toponymy.

title: Real-world loan-profile: Akkadian/Semitic -> English (light coverage; Adûnaic dependency)

Hypothetical/light empirical loan-profile for Semitic donors into English. Unlike Arabic->Spanish, this is mostly *modern* scholarly loans (Layard-era and later: ziggurat, dragoman, sheikh, alcohol via Arabic) rather than substrate-toponymic.

title: Real-world loan-profile: Arabic -> Spanish (Andalucía toponym layer)
description:
Mine the empirical Arabic->Spanish loan-adaptation profile from Iberian toponymy. The most documented foreign->native toponymic adaptation outside English: every Andalusian alc- (al-qasr 'castle'), Wadi-/Guad- (wādī 'river'), Med- (madīna 'city'), Ben-/Bin- (ibn 'son of') place name is a documented loan adaptation pathway.

Independent value: 'we can use any real world language to see how loan words incorporate' — this is one of the cleanest empirical loan-pair datasets in human linguistics. Studying it informs the adaptation algorithm's general design even without a fantasy use case.

Composes-with-epic value: unlocks Iberian/Mediterranean-flavored fantasy generators (Reconquista-feel, Andalusi-feel) as future fantasy packs.

- Scholarly references: Asín Palacios 'Contribución a la toponimia árabe de España' (1944); Pocklington's Arabic-Spanish toponymy papers

Output: arabic -> spanish -> [medieval-spanish, modern-spanish] adaptation template + calibration set. Could feed back into Phase 3d's mining infrastructure as a second donor->recipient pair to validate the approach generalizes.

title: Shavian Phase 6: evaluation harness (corpus + round-trip accuracy + heteronym accuracy baselines)
description:
Stand up the measurement infrastructure so transliteration quality is tracked over time, and so this generator can be compared against the existing public Shavian transliterators that motivated the work.

DELIVERABLES:

1) Test corpus.
   - 3-5 hand-curated paragraphs in 'wyrd/generators/shavian/data/eval_corpus.json':
     - General prose (Wikipedia excerpt)
     - Dialogue with contractions
     - Technical text with abbreviations + numerals
     - A passage dense in known heteronyms (assembled deliberately)
     - A passage dense in known homophones
   - Each paragraph has a gold-standard Shavian transliteration (initially produced by the pipeline, then human-reviewed).

2) Metrics (a 'wyrd shavian eval' CLI subcommand):
   - Round-trip word accuracy (English → Shavian → English, % of words recovered correctly).
   - Heteronym sense accuracy (% of heteronym tokens where the correct sense was chosen, measured against gold).
   - Homophone disambiguation accuracy (% of homophone tokens recovered correctly on the reverse path).
   - OOV rate (% of tokens that hit the G2P fallback rather than ReadLex).

3) Baseline run + report.
   - Run the eval after Phase 5 lands, record numbers in 'wyrd/generators/shavian/COVERAGE.md' (matching the kenning generator's convention).
   - Compare against at least one public Shavian transliterator (link to its output on the same corpus, if licensing allows).

4) Regression gate.
   - Add a CI test that runs the eval and fails if any metric drops more than 2 percentage points from the recorded baseline. (Adjust the threshold per metric if too tight in practice.)

DEPENDS ON: Phase 1, Phase 3, Phase 5 (the polish work materially affects round-trip numbers, so eval is most useful after polish lands).

title: Shavian Phase 5: polish — namer dot, numerals, abbreviations, round-trip preservation
description:
Handle the edge cases that turn a working transliterator into a usable one for TTRPG prop documents.

SCOPE:

1) Namer dot for proper nouns.
   - Shavian convention: a leading 'namer dot' (·) marks proper nouns ('London' → ·𐑤𐑳𐑯𐑛𐑩𐑯).
   - Detection: POS tagger should already mark NNP / NNPS. Use that as the trigger.
   - Reverse: when consuming Shavian, recover capitalization from the namer dot.

2) Numerals.
   - Shavian has no native digits — convention is to either (a) keep Arabic digits inline, or (b) spell out as words.
   - Default: keep digits inline (simpler, lossless round-trip).
   - Provide an option in input_schema to spell-out small numbers (<100) for stylistic / fantasy flavor.

3) Abbreviations.
   - 'Mr.', 'Dr.', 'St.', 'etc.', 'i.e.' — expand before tagging (use a small lookup table).
   - Document which abbreviations are handled; everything else passes through unchanged.

4) Round-trip preservation.
   - Whitespace exact preservation (including newlines and multiple spaces if present).
   - Punctuation passthrough.
   - Capitalization: recovered via namer-dot path for proper nouns; sentence-initial capitalization handled by detecting sentence boundaries on the reverse path.

5) Apostrophes / contractions.
   - 'don't', 'it's', 'they're' — ReadLex should cover these directly. If not, fall back to splitting and recombining.

TESTS:
- Round-trip a curated mixed-content paragraph (proper nouns, numbers, contractions, abbreviations) and assert byte-for-byte equality (where possible) or token-level equality.
- Heteronym-with-namer-dot edge cases (e.g. 'Wind' as a name, 'Mr. Lead').

DEPENDS ON: Phase 1, Phase 3, Phase 4.

title: wyrd-x82p Phase 2b.1 perf: add source_doc index to toponym_attestation
description: Gemini PR #214 round-3 finding: idx_attestation_unique has source_doc as the LAST composite column, so the bulk preflight SELECT WHERE source_doc=? falls back to full-table scan. At current scale (~5-50K attestations/source × 32 sources, ~10ms full scan), the N+1→bulk-SELECT fix already dominates the perf win. But as Phase 2b.2 brings full-corpus extraction online (multi-million mentions), adding a dedicated index on toponym_attestation(source_doc) would let SQLite use it directly. Requires schema migration.

title: _extract_attestation_pairs source-chain guard over-suppresses in body-text context
description:
Discovered during wyrd-x82p Phase 1 review (PR #212 silent-failure-hunter).

The _SOURCE_CHAIN_PRECEDING_YEAR_RE + _SOURCE_CHAIN_FOLLOWING_YEAR_RE guard in _extract_attestation_pairs() (lexicon.py:3681) suppresses (form, year) matches when form is preceded by '<year> ' AND followed by ', <year>'. This guards against source-name FPs like '1539 Wills, 1544 LP' where 'Wills' is a source name in a multi-source chain.

The guard was calibrated for short toponym_etymology.notes strings where the pattern is rare and the FP is the common case. In long body-text contexts (PR #212's reverse_search_source), the pattern is COMMON and represents legitimate attestation chains: '1086 Suttone, 1210' is two real attestations of Suttone, not a source-name FP.

Current effect on wyrd-x82p Phase 1: an unknown number of valid (form, year) pairs are silently dropped before they reach toponym lookup. They don't show up in unmatched_samples — they're invisible.

Options:
1. Add context_is_body parameter to _extract_attestation_pairs; disable guard when True
2. Make the guard smarter (e.g., check if the form is in the toponym corpus before suppressing)
3. Add suppressed_by_chain counter to surface what's being dropped, leave guard semantics unchanged

Option 1 is cleanest but risks admitting source-name FPs in body text. Option 3 is observability-only — operator can decide based on data.

Phase 2 of wyrd-x82p (LLM extraction) will catch most of what Phase 1's guard misses anyway. This ticket tracks the underlying pattern-based extractor refinement.
close_reason: Verified done: context_is_body guard refinement + telemetry decoupling + tests (bc72910e).

title: Re-mine Watson 1926 + similar high-hallucination sources via bigger LLM context
description:
Discovered during wyrd-1hpc context-refill pilot:

watson_1926_celtic_place_names_of_scotland's flagged short_quotes (117 across PR #190 baseline) are predominantly LLM-hallucinated commentary rather than truncated quotes. Refill recovery rate was only 51.3% (vs 73-89% on the other top-5 sources), and 100% of the failures were 'long anchor not in source, short anchor also not in source' — i.e. the LLM-emitted prose simply doesn't exist in Watson's body text.

Watson 1926's academic prose style appears to elicit LLM summarization rather than quoting. Same pattern shows up at lower rates across all sources (~10-27% hallucinated). Aggregate across top-5 was 150 hallucinated cases (out of 806 flagged).

Approach: re-mine with a bigger-context LLM (qwen3.5:35b-a3b or claude-sonnet-4-5). Bigger context window should let the LLM emit verbatim quotes rather than summarized commentary.

Acceptance: post-pass re-run of `lexicon audit-short-quotes` shows the residual flagged count on watson_1926 cut by ≥75%, and the source body now contains the cited text (verifiable via the same anchor-search method).

The wyrd-1hpc context-refill closed 539 of the 806 flagged across top-4 sources (66% coverage) without LLM cost. Watson 1926 (117 flags) + the ~150 hallucinated residuals across the other 4 sources are the remaining work.

title: Bundle export: <lang>_english_shaped + _transliteration siblings absent (wyrd-vsrn Phase 2c regression?)
description:
Discovered during wyrd-j43l bundle re-export:

The bundle has 0 word-level <lang>_english_shaped and <lang>_transliteration sibling fields, despite:
- 48,070 etymon rows carrying english_shaped values in the live DB

Reproduction:
1. wyrd kenning lexicon export-meanings --output /tmp/test-bundle.json
2. python3 -c "import json; b=json.load(open('/tmp/test-bundle.json')); n=sum(1 for s in b['subjects'] for w in s.get('words',[]) for k in w if k.endswith('_english_shaped')); print(n)"

Not a blocker for wyrd-j43l deploy — the bundle is otherwise healthy and the bundle SPA consumers gracefully degrade on missing siblings. But it means the user-visible multi-script rendering feature (etymological-provenance panel) won't have english_shaped data to display.

Should investigate the family-collector → bucket-absorb chain. Could be:

title: Add toponym_attestation to DIFF_REBUILD_TABLES + extend _l2_state_snapshot
description:
pr-test-analyzer on PR #204 flagged that DIFF_REBUILD_TABLES (wyrd/generators/kenning/jsonl_build.py:45) doesn't include toponym_attestation. The diff-rebuild operator workflow (lexicon rebuild-from-jsonl --diff) is the human-facing guard against round-trip regressions; without attestation in the monitored set, a future regression that silently drops all attestations would produce a zero-delta diff and go undetected.

PR #204 closes the dump-side gap. Now that attestation round-trips, it's safe (and necessary) to add it to the diff guard.

1. Add 'toponym_attestation' to DIFF_REBUILD_TABLES
2. Extend _l2_state_snapshot in tests/test_kenning_jsonl_build.py to include attestation rows
3. Verify the format_diff_rebuild output reads sensibly when attestation count drops/rises
4. Bundle pre-existing similar gaps if any (check toponym_etymology coverage)

This is pre-existing — was out of scope for PR #204.
close_reason: Verified done: toponym_attestation added to DIFF_REBUILD_TABLES + _l2_state_snapshot extended (bc72910e).

title: Add dump-side orphan-attestation telemetry (counter + warn)
description:
silent-failure-hunter on PR #204 flagged that dump_all_sources silently drops attestation rows whose source_doc routes nowhere (no direct source_id match, no registered prefix). The build side has attestation_orphans telemetry; the dump side has nothing.

Risk: a new ingester or a typo introduces source_docs that don't match any pattern, and the rows disappear from JSONL dumps. Six months later, a lexicon rebuild-from-jsonl produces a smaller DB with no explanation.

Implementation sketch:
- One-shot query at the end of dump_all_sources counting toponym_attestation rows whose source_doc neither equals any source.id nor starts with any registered prefix
- click.echo a warning with the count when non-zero
- Optionally surface as a return value for programmatic callers

Out of scope on PR #204 (Phase A — code skeleton); filing here for Phase B.

title: Refactor _insert_etymon — extract _merge_etymon_conflict helper
description:
Per complexity-reviewer on PR #203: _insert_etymon grew from ~22 lines to 68 lines after the wyrd-pcsj upsert fix. The else: branch (lines 172-204 — SELECT existing id + defensive None-check + UPDATE non-key scalars) is a self-contained unit that could be extracted to a module-level _merge_etymon_conflict(conn, payload, cols) -> int helper. That would bring _insert_etymon back to ~25 lines.

Also bundle (per silent-failure-hunter same PR):
* Document _NON_SCHOLAR_SOURCES + the _ETYMON_INSERT_COLUMNS allowlist explicitly so the L2/L3 boundary intent is clearer at the call site.
* Pre-existing concern: jsonl_build.table_counts catches sqlite3.OperationalError silently with no logging — a 'database is locked' or schema mismatch makes has_any_delta return True and fail CI with no diagnosis. Add logger.warning.
* Pre-existing concern: jsonl_build._insert_toponym uses plain INSERT — currently safe (toponym table has no UNIQUE constraint), but document the asymmetry with _insert_etymon's upsert so a future schema change adding a UNIQUE to toponym doesn't silently regress.

Tests added in PR #203 cover the merge contract; the refactor should be regression-safe.

title: Refactor: extract helpers in diff-bundle command + bundle_diff module
description:
complexity-reviewer + import-reviewer flagged three deferrable refactors in PR #201 (wyrd-w3x0). All were explicitly marked as 'beads ticket / deferral acceptable' by the reviewers; bundling them into one follow-up:

1. **format_bundle_diff is too long** (bundle_diff.py, ~93 lines). The 'emit capped list with ... and N more' pattern repeats identically for added/removed/changed subjects. Extract a module-level _emit_capped_list helper, plus a _format_subjects_section and _format_other_fields_section.

2. **lang-threshold parser duplication** (cli.py). The 16-line lang-threshold parsing block in lexicon_diff_bundle is a verbatim copy of the same block in lexicon_export_meanings (around cli.py:1311-1330). Extract a module-level _parse_lang_thresholds(specs, use_preset) helper and call it from both commands so they can't drift.

3. **lexicon_diff_bundle body is too long** (cli.py, ~90 lines across 6 phases: validate flags, load joiners, L1 bulk ingest, L2 replay, L3 enrichment, export+assemble+diff). Identified two natural split points: _rebuild_lexicon_db(rebuilt_path, jsonl_dir, fetch_bulk, skip_bulk) and _assemble_bundle_dict(db, ...). Note the tmpdir lifetime needs to outlive the rebuild → bundle flow, so the helpers may need to accept the open tmpdir path rather than create their own.

Scope each as a separate commit so reviewers can land them independently. Tests already cover the surface: the round-trip test (wyrd-xrnw / test_kenning_hidb_phase3_round_trip.py) + the bundle-diff tests (test_kenning_bundle_diff.py + test_kenning_diff_bundle_cli.py) catch any behavioral regression from the extractions.

title: Re-mine top-5 short_quote-truncation offenders with larger LLM context window
description:
The wyrd-bd68 audit (docs/audits/2026-05-13_short_quote_truncation.md, committed in PR #190) identified 2,038 probably-truncated short_quote citations across 51 sources. Top-5 sources account for ~37% of the total flagged:

  mawer_1920_northumberland_durham      283 / 1165 (24.3%)
  joyce_1898_irish_names_vol3           151 /  429 (35.2%)
  ekwall_1922_lancashire                134 /  609 (22.0%)
  joyce_1913_irish_names_of_places      121 /  332 (36.4%)
  watson_1926_celtic_place_names...     117 /  272 (43.0%)

Approach options:
1. Re-mine with larger context window (qwen3.5:35b-a3b or anthropic claude-sonnet-4-5) — recovers the cut-off citation context at the cost of LLM compute.
2. Context-snippet refill: pull missing context from sources/<book>.txt via the citation page number (wyrd-9kh.4/.5 infrastructure exists for this).

Acceptance: post-pass re-run of `lexicon audit-short-quotes` shows the top-5 offenders' truncated counts cut by ≥75%. Append the new snapshot to docs/audits/.

Why now: audit snapshot is the evidence; the connection between audit and re-mining work fades if not filed contemporaneously. Per PR #190 reviewer recommendation.

Linked to wyrd-eni4 epic (Phase-2-ish curation pass).
notes:
PR #211 merged 2026-05-15T23:27Z after 9 review rounds.

Final outcome:
- 489 truncated short_quotes refilled across top-4 sources (Mawer 1920, Joyce 1898, Joyce 1913, Ekwall 1922)
- 200 cases classified as hallucinated (LLM-emitted prose not in source body — needs LLM re-mine, separate ticket)
- No LLM cost (refill is text-search against sources/<book>.txt)
- 37 tests, 0 unresolved review threads, full suite 2798+

Sample fix (old-english:dcum, Mawer 1920):
  BEFORE: 200 chars truncated at '1268'
  AFTER:  ~270 chars with Akum 1414, S.R., Yorks parallel, OE etymology

Architecture highlights:
- _trim_to_terminal_char ensures refilled tails end at .!?"')]} so the audit doesn't re-flag (idempotency)
- _MIN_ANCHOR_LEN=20 prevents short-anchor false positives (applied to BOTH primary 80-char and fallback 40-char paths after round-5 fanout caught the bypass)
- _unique_find rejects ambiguous matches (>1 occurrence in source body)
- source_body_path() module helper centralizes the sources/<id>.txt naming convention (post-round-9 DRY refactor) AND the path-traversal hardening
- SQL filter `length(short_quote) >= 200` pushes the truncation-length floor to DB
- Streaming cursor iteration + executemany() bound memory on large citation tables
- _load_source_body returns None for missing/UnicodeDecodeError/OSError/empty-body
- CLI uses LexiconDB context manager; report content goes to stdout; missing-source warning fires in default mode too

Review iteration (rounds 1-9):
- Round 1: 30 threads (Gemini + 6 agents); covered baseline correctness
- Round 5: 24 threads (6-agent re-fanout) — caught HIGH bugs the early rounds missed:
  * Fallback anchor bypassed _MIN_ANCHOR_LEN after .strip()
  * Two tests passed for the wrong reason (untested code paths)
  * Round-4 warning condition was too broad (false positives on all-hallucinated sources)
- Rounds 6-9: 1-3 findings each (perf, path traversal, source iteration, DRY)
- Round 10: clean

Filed for follow-up:

title: Dedupe exact-duplicate toponym_etymology rows from re-run LLM mining
description:
Per Gemini review of PR #175 round 2: data/mining/bannister_1916_herefordshire.jsonl has exact-duplicate etymology_element rows (e.g., 'Cart@Herefordshire' / 'ac-tun' appears twice on lines 309-310; 'Dom@Herefordshire' / 'Ceabba-bank' twice on lines 320-321).

Root cause: toponym_etymology table has no UNIQUE constraint on (toponym_id, source_id, historical_form, element-list-shape). When mining is re-run with the same model+prompt against the same source, the writer inserts a second identical row.

Two fix paths (not mutually exclusive):
1. Add UNIQUE constraint to toponym_etymology preventing exact dupes (probably (toponym_id, source_id, COALESCE(historical_form,''), provenance)).
2. Dedupe at dump time — content-equal etymology_element rows fold to one canonical-state row.

Currently the dump faithfully preserves what's in the DB (round-trip claim intact), so dedup is a separate data-quality pass. Adjacent to wyrd-lene (hallucinated toponyms) but operates on duplicate rows, not on wrong rows.

title: Expose public phonology_chain_for() API; stop importing _PHONOLOGY_* privates from lexicon.py
description:
During wyrd-pmne review, the generator-contract reviewer flagged that wyrd/generators/kenning/language_quality.py imports three module-private symbols across the lexicon.py boundary:

- _phonology_rule_form
- _PHONOLOGY_FAMILY_CHAINS
- _PHONOLOGY_LANGUAGE_ALIASES

These are leading-underscore private symbols (per Python convention) and the cross-module import freezes their names as a de-facto public API. Any future refactor (consolidating chain registration, moving rules into phonology_rules.py) will have to update the reporting code as a side effect.

Recommendation: expose a public API in phonology_rules.py (or a new wyrd/generators/kenning/phonology.py module):

- phonology_chain_for(language: str) -> tuple[str, tuple[str, ...]] | None
- phonology_rule_form(canonical_form, from_language, to_language) -> str | None

Then have language_quality.py consume those public functions, and gradually migrate the lexicon.py call sites too.

Not blocking — wyrd-pmne shipped with the function-local-import pattern, which keeps the blast radius small. But the convention violation is real and worth cleaning up before another consumer (KenningEraMap explainer? Tier-4 mining tool?) adopts the same pattern.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #171. phonology_rules.py now exposes FAMILY_CHAINS, LANGUAGE_ALIASES, chain_for(), resolve_language(), rule_form() as the public API. language_quality.py + lexicon.py consume the public API; no more privately-named cross-module imports. 757 affected tests pass.

Options:
1. Synthesize at metric time: call _phonology_rule_form over each etymon's chain and count truthy returns. Slow (1.4M etymons × N chain hops); cache or sample.
2. Persist Tier 4 outputs as a synthetic etymon_era_reflex row during bundle export so the metric has data to count. Mirrors wyrd-jbcu's source-tagged design.
3. Add a separate 'Tier 4 (synthesized)' line to the F breakdown that calls the live function for bundle-shipped etymons only (denominator-friendly).
