title: etymon_citation: future re-mine could create duplicate (etymon, source, NULL) row alongside backfilled (etymon, source, page) row
description:
From PR #36 review: the unique index is etymon_citation(etymon_id, source_id, COALESCE(page, '')). After wyrd-azv backfills page='15' on an existing row, a future re-mine via add_citation() (which always passes page=None) would insert a NEW row at (etymon, source, NULL) without conflicting — splitting the same evidence into two citation rows.

Possible fixes (not blocking on v1):
1. Have add_citation() check for any existing (etymon, source) row first and skip if one exists.
2. Or have the mining writer pass a page=NULL with INSERT OR IGNORE that treats any existing row as the de-dup target (would need ON CONFLICT clause restructure).
3. Or document that re-mining should always run backfill-pages immediately after.

Affects: wyrd/generators/kenning/lexicon.py add_citation; wyrd/generators/kenning/data/lexicon.sql idx_etymon_citation_unique.

title: Backfill: ambiguous_match counter when source_quote could match multiple body positions
description:
From PR #36 review: backfill_citation_pages uses str.find which always returns the leftmost match. If a stock phrase ('See Plate III.') happens to appear in multiple entries, the page silently resolves to the first occurrence — which may not be the entry the citation actually came from.

Acceptable for v1 because:
- Real source_quote excerpts are 200-500 chars and tend to be entry-unique
- Misattribution is to a NEARBY page (citations cluster by alphabet), not a random page
- Better to have an approximately-correct page than NULL

Future improvement: count matches up front, increment ambiguous_match when n>1, and either pick the first / log to a separate audit table / require disambiguation. Per D24 the count should land in a queryable column or audit row, not stdout-only.

Code pointer: wyrd/generators/kenning/lexicon.py _resolve_page inner function.

title: Widen attested_year validator range to capture Roman/Gaulish-period citations (currently 800-1700)
description:
The D5-1 attested_year validator (in llm_extractor.py: _ATTESTED_YEAR_MIN=800, _ATTESTED_YEAR_MAX=1700) was sized for British/Continental Norman-era place-names (Domesday 1086 onward). On Roman/Gaulish-period sources like d'Arbois 1890 'Recherches sur l'origine de la propriété foncière (période celtique et période romaine)', the 800-floor blocks legitimate Roman-empire and Frankish-era citations.

Concrete: d'Arbois 1890 smoke (30 entries) yielded 12 accepted but 8 rejected, with rejection reason counts: attested_year_out_of_range=8, attested_year_not_int=10. Multiple rejections per entry. The 'out_of_range' rejections are losing legitimate Roman charters (e.g. 'une charte de l'année 786' would land < 800). The 'not_int' rejections are model emitting strings like '856 (?)' rather than integers — separate bug, see below.

Proposed:
1. Widen _ATTESTED_YEAR_MIN from 800 to 100 — covers Roman empire, Visigothic, early Merovingian. Below 100 is still too noisy (folio numbers and page numbers crash into legitimate range).
2. Tighten the SYSTEM_PROMPT 'attested_forms' section to emphasize INTEGER format — current prompt says 'integer 800-1700' in the schema example but apparently models still emit strings like '856 (?)' or '856 ca.'. Add an explicit example: WRONG: {form: 'X', year: '856 (?)'}. RIGHT: {form: 'X', year: 856}.
3. Update tests to cover the new range bounds (100 floor + 99 below boundary).
4. After the change merges, re-mine d'Arbois 1890 (idempotent, cheap) to recover the rejected Roman-period rows.

Ownership: extractor-layer (validator + prompt) is in the research-thread Claude's territory per the 2026-05-02 division. Companion tests in tests/test_kenning_llm_extractor.py.

OUT OF SCOPE:
- The cap stays at 1700 (post-Restoration sources are likely citing publication years, not attestation years).
- Per-source range overrides (would add complexity for a single use case).
close_reason: Merged in PR #42 (squash 3ca119b). Widened _ATTESTED_YEAR_MIN from 800 to 100 to capture Roman-era / early-Merovingian dated attestations on Romance-Celtic-substrate sources. SYSTEM_PROMPT tightened with explicit RIGHT/WRONG examples for JSON-integer-not-string year format. 466 tests pass; ruff clean; CI green; loop converged in 1 round (agents clean, Gemini rate-limited but no actionable feedback).

title: Tier-2 review candidate query: include Haiku-Tier-1 rows for non-Celtic books
description:
The 'wyrd kenning lexicon review --provider gemini' command filters its candidate query to provider='ollama' rows (per INGESTION.md Stage 5 'review path's candidate query specifically targets Ollama-tagged rows'). This was correct when D2/D13 framed the matrix as:
- English: Qwen Tier-1 -> Gemini Tier-2 review
- Celtic: Haiku Tier-1 (already strong); skip Tier-2

But the matrix has evolved: some non-Celtic books are now Haiku-Tier-1 because the content shape benefits from it (Bannister 1916 Welsh-Marches NF, Harrison 1898 Liverpool, etc.). Those books currently miss Tier-2 review entirely — Gemini's hedge-recognition advantage (D14) doesn't reach them.

Proposed scope:
1. Extend the candidate query to ALSO include Haiku-Tier-1 rows where the source's primary language is in (old-english, modern-english, norman-french, mixed). Identifying the source language could come from the source row metadata or a per-source policy table.
2. Default behavior on existing English-Qwen books unchanged.
3. Behavior on pure Celtic books (Joyce, Watson, Gillies, Macbain) unchanged — still skip Haiku rows.
4. Add a per-source override flag if the heuristic is wrong: 'wyrd kenning lexicon review --include-haiku --book <id>'.

Out of scope:
- A 'rerun-Haiku-with-different-prompt' loop. That's a separate refactor.

Why now: filed as part of the 2026-05-02 mining_run audit pass. Bannister 1916 (35% Haiku accept) and Harrison 1898 (37% Haiku accept) are both candidates to benefit. Filed alongside wyrd-??? (Bannister review) which can either run after this fix or before via a per-source override.

See /tmp/wyrd-corpus-research-2026-05-02.md for the audit summary.

title: Investigate Harrison 1898 Liverpool 33% rejection rate (Haiku Tier-1)
description:
Harrison 1898 Liverpool was mined Tier-1 Haiku and shows an anomalous rejection-rate profile: 56 rejected / 170 parsed = 33% reject. Normal band per INGESTION.md is 5-15%; >=25% means investigate.

For comparison, Skeat 1904 Hertfordshire (already noted in INGESTION.md as a format-anomaly outlier) is at 26% reject. Harrison is even worse.

Diagnostic order:
1. Check rejection_reasons distribution: SELECT by_failure_json FROM mining_run WHERE source_id='harrison_1898_liverpool';
2. Sample 10 rejected rows; check whether the rejected forms are (a) OCR-garbled but legitimate (book-side issue) or (b) hallucinated by the model (model-side issue).
3. If (a), the form-in-body validator is correctly rejecting OCR-garbled forms — no fix; the book is partial-loss and we accept the corpus contribution we already have.
4. If (b), investigate prompt regression on this content shape; possibly retry with stronger prompt + Gemini review.

NOT a candidate for blind re-pass: a different model on the same OCR'd body will likely produce the same rejection profile.

Re-pass would only help if the 33% reject is model-overreach rather than book-side OCR damage. Diagnose first.
notes: Closed 2026-05-05. Harrison 1898 Liverpool Tier-2 Gemini review ran via the wyrd-eca --include-haiku flag: 22 reviewed, 8 written, 12 declined, 2 rejected. 36% Gemini-on-Haiku accept rate. Net +8 Gemini-tagged rows. The original 33% rejection-rate diagnostic concern (Tier-1 Haiku) didn't propagate into Tier-2 — Gemini's hedge-recognition didn't flag a content-shape problem. Closing without a fix; the 33% Tier-1 reject rate is bounded by the 67% accept rate which already gave the corpus 56 toponym_etymology rows.

description:

Initial OCR fetch caught only the front phonological essay; the back-half dictionary structure is title-confirmed but not body-density-confirmed yet.

Source: archive.org/details/essaisurlepatois00joreuoft (222 pages, full DJVU TXT)

Smoke-test the DICTIONARY portion (find where the phonological essay ends and the alphabetical section begins) before committing to a full mining pass. If body density is acceptable, proceed Tier-1 Haiku per D13 (Romance content; Norman dialect).

Importance: Channel Islands NF probe was confirmed barren in PD window (Le Maistre 1966 not PD until ~2036+). Joret 1881 is the ONLY remaining direct Norman-French dialect dictionary candidate among PD sources. Combined with Bannister 1916 (Welsh-Marches NF, already shipped per PR #22), this would close out wyrd-hub's PD coverage.

See /tmp/wyrd-corpus-research-2026-05-02.md for the wyrd-hub status update.
notes:
2026-05-03 (research session): Probed sources/joret_1881_patois_normand_bessin.txt (fetched from IA: archive.org/details/essaisurlepatois00joreuoft, 222 pages). Parser found 79 entries from the alphabetical dictionary section.

CRITICAL finding: Joret 1881 is a NORMAN DIALECT word-dictionary, NOT a toponymic dictionary. Sample entries:
- 'Etande, v. a. : étendre. R, extendere.' (Norman 'étende' ← Latin extendere)
- 'Foche, fouache, s. f. : petit pain au beurre. R. focacia.' (Norman dialect word for a pastry)
- 'FoRTEUNE, s. f. : fortune, richesse. R. fortuna.' (Norman form of 'fortune')

The 'suivi d'un dictionnaire étymologique' from the title is etymology of DIALECT WORDS, not place-names. The original wyrd-hub framing assumed it was toponym-shaped because the book covers Bessin (a Norman region), but Joret was doing dialectology, not onomastics.

Pipeline mismatch identical to Troude 1876 / Le Gonidec / Châlons-Loth — language dictionaries fit the wyrd-4rt Wiktionary-style ingestion path (entry → standalone etymon row), not the existing mine-llm path (toponym → etymology breakdown).

For NF expansion (wyrd-hub) this means:
- The Joret 1881 candidate doesn't yield through the existing mining pipeline.
- Bessin-area NF is still likely the strongest geographic angle — needs a TOPONYMIC source. Possible alternatives to probe: a Bessin/Caen-area cartulaire, Beaurepaire's Normandy place-name studies (1830s-1850s, PD), or a département-toponymique like Joret might list separately.
- After wyrd-4rt's Wiktionary pipeline lands, Joret 1881's 79 dialect entries become directly mineable for Norman-French word morphemes (relevant to wyrd-fmg breton + norman expansion).

Closing as 'probe complete, defer mining until pipeline support'.

Pipeline-mismatch — needs wyrd-4rt-style language-dictionary ingestion, not the existing mine-llm toponym path. Source fetched + characterized; 79 entries available for the Wiktionary-style pipeline when it lands. Bessin area still strongest NF angle; needs different source.

title: Mine Le Gonidec/Villemarqué 1850 augmented edition (second-witness Breton)
description:
La Villemarqué's 1850 augmented edition of Le Gonidec's Dictionnaire breton-français. Cleaner OCR than the 1821 original (later typeface, fewer accent-mojibake artifacts). Adds a preface, additions, and Welsh + Gaelic cognates.

Source: archive.org/details/dictionnairebre00unkngoog (614 pages, full DJVU TXT)

Tier-1 Haiku per D13.

Role: second-witness layer over the Troude 1876 corpus (filed separately). Pushes the highest-frequency Breton morphemes from 1-2 witnesses to 2-3 (D4 promotion threshold). Run AFTER Troude 1876 since the witness rollup wants the larger source first.

Lower priority than Troude/Loth because the marginal value is per-morpheme-witness-uplift rather than new-morpheme-discovery. See /tmp/wyrd-corpus-research-2026-05-02.md.

title: Wire D5: (language × era) era-aware register cells
description:
DECISIONS.md D5 promises any (language × era) cell — Old English at ~900 AD = Hædan-tūn; Old English modernized = Hadenham; Latin at empire = Pons Aquae. Currently the runtime has only the (language) axis; era is implicit in the morpheme set, no cells.

This is the biggest scope of the chain. Probably wants a separate epic.

Scope (rough):
1. Era tagging on etymons in the lexicon (pre-1066, Domesday, late-medieval, early-modern, modern). Mining-time field from the source's date or the form's expected period.
2. Per-(language × era) sub-proportions: language alone today, language × era after.
3. Phonology: era-specific orthography rules (OE ƿ vs w, modern-English collapse rules).
4. Sound-change rules library (separate ticket wyrd-4i6) is the engine for converting between era cells.
5. CLI / API: 'wyrd kenning generate english --era 900' or '--era pre-1066'.

Acceptance: at default (modern era), behavior unchanged; user can request a specific era and get morphemes drawn from that period.

Caveat: substantial work. May want to split into (a) era tagging on etymons (data), (b) era-aware proportions (sampling), (c) era-aware orthography (surface form), (d) cross-era sound-change rules — separate tickets.
notes:
2026-05-02 update (research session): Architecture design + epic split filed. Per the prior handoff's 'probably wants splitting into 3-4 tickets' note, decomposed D5 into 4 layers:

- wyrd-3ux (D5-1): Mine attested years from source bodies via regex post-mining stage. Foundation. Adds attested_year column to etymon_text_match. LLM-free, idempotent, reversible.
- wyrd-38d (D5-2): Era-cell mapping + filtered sampling on (language × era) axis. Defines era cells per family + --era CLI/JSON param that filters morpheme inventory. Depends on D5-1.
- wyrd-lyp (D5-3): Era-aware bundle export + runtime cell selection. Adds <lang>_era arrays per D26; wires Meaning.pick_era_form. Depends on D5-2.
- wyrd-4i6 (D5-4 = pre-existing): Cross-era sound-change rules library. Independent of D5-1/2/3. Required only for 'Old English modernized'-style rule-based surface derivation; D5-1+2+3 ship era axis WITHOUT it (era-attested-only forms).

Approach choice for v1: Layer-2 path (c) — era is a generation-time FILTER on morpheme inventory; tag-co-occurrence stays per-culture (existing proportions JSONs unchanged). Cheaper than per-(lang × era) tag-co-occurrence; ships immediately on D5-1 data. Per-era tag-co-occurrence is v2.

Open questions (see design doc):
1. Era cell granularity (proposed 4-5 cells per family) — confirm
2. Era as separate axis vs language-enum split — confirmed separate axis (preserves D8 lemma identity)
3. Year-extraction prompt vs regex — regex (path C) for v1, prompt re-mining deferred
4. Default era on no '--era' flag — keep current bit-stable behavior
5. Bundle size — ~30-50KB extra, negligible
6. celtic enum sub-division (Brythonic vs Goidelic era cells differ) — open

Full design rationale, layer-by-layer trade-offs, PD source survey for D5-4 sound-change rules, and risk register in /tmp/wyrd-d5-era-axis-design-2026-05-02.md.

title: Norman-French corpus expansion: Channel Islands + EPNS Southern-county targeting
description:
Norman-French is the thinnest mined language (111 lemmas at >=1 witness, only 7 at >=2, 2 at >=3). The structural reason is corpus availability — most modern Norman-French scholarship is post-WW2 and still in copyright. Two PD-friendly directions:

(a) Channel Islands toponymy: Jersey, Guernsey, Sark were the closest English-controlled territory and retained Norman dialect into the 20th century. PD scholarship from the Société Jersiaise / Société Guernesiaise era (early 1900s) likely covers Channel Islands place names. Need to probe for what's been digitized (Internet Archive, archive.org/details/jersey, etc.).

(b) EPNS Southern-county volumes with heavier Norman strata: Sussex (already partial via mawer_stenton_1930_sussex + roberts_1914_sussex), plus Kent, Hampshire, and East Anglia. Norman conquest impact peaked in the South-East; OE-county dicts under-weight that layer.

Suggested first steps: (i) probe Channel Islands archive.org for PD place-name dictionaries (Yves Falla, J. Le Maistre, etc.), (ii) check which EPNS Sussex/Kent/Hampshire/East-Anglian volumes are PD (1928 cutoff plus author-death rules), (iii) mine via Tier-1 Haiku per D13 if Celtic-French boundary content, otherwise Qwen.

Surfaced when discussing PR #15 (per-language witness thresholds): NF gets only +4 words moving from uniform-3 to the recommended preset because the population at w>=2 is already exhausted at 7 lemmas. Threshold can't help; need more sources.
notes:
2026-05-02 update (research session): Channel Islands NF probe is structurally barren in PD window — ALREADY confirmed in prior wyrd-hub note (Carey 1904, Ansted 1893, Berry 1815, Société Jersiaise Bulletins were all essay/travelogue). Frank Le Maistre's foundational 1966 Dictionnaire Jersiais-Français is not PD until ~2036+ per UK life+70.

NEW finding (research probe): Joret 1881 'Essai sur le patois Normand du Bessin; suivi d'un dictionnaire étymologique' (archive.org/details/essaisurlepatois00joreuoft, 222 p) — has an etymological dictionary section per title + addenda. Filed as wyrd-8m9. Smoke-test the dictionary section (after the front phonological essay) before committing to a full mining pass.

Combined with Bannister 1916 (Welsh-Marches NF, already shipped per PR #22), Joret 1881 closes out wyrd-hub's PD source coverage. Channel Islands direction should be considered closed; Welsh-Marches + Bessin are the surviving PD angles for NF expansion.

Full context in /tmp/wyrd-corpus-research-2026-05-02.md.

title: export-meanings: narrow per-reflex language arrays via reflex_etymon links
description:
In wyrd/generators/kenning/lexicon.py:_build_words_for_group, every reflex's word entry currently uses the subject-wide combined_forms across all families in the group. That's too wide: a reflex like '-don' should only carry the etymons it's actually linked to via reflex_etymon (here: 'dun'), not also celtic_mix forms from a sibling reflex like 'Bre-' that lives under the same Hill subject.

Per the original meanings.json shape (e.g. the 'Alder tree' subject), each word's language slots are reflex-specific — '-farne' has only celtic_mix; 'Alder-' has only old_english; 'Orle-' has both. seed_from_meanings preserves this via per-(reflex,etymon) links in reflex_etymon.

The right fix is per-reflex etymon lookup: for each reflex R seen in the subject, find R's directly-linked etymons via reflex_etymon, roll each to its family root, and emit only those families' forms grouped by language. Synthesized words (families without any reflex) keep their own forms_by_lang only.

Why deferred: this requires restructuring _gather_family or _build_words_for_group to thread reflex_links through. Functionally the runtime decomposer/generator works either way — the over-wide language arrays only affect explanation prose (a generated '-don' name's explanation might claim celtic origins it doesn't have). Cosmetic v1 issue; tracked here to fix when the lemma+variants weighting refactor lands.

Surfaced by Gemini in PR #14 review (comment 3176293576): https://github.com/521-studios/wyrd/pull/14#discussion_r2710906366
close_reason: Fixed in PR #14 round-2 (commit f07d23f). _gather_family collects per-reflex linked etymon ids + member descendants; _build_words_for_group walks each reflex's linked etymons + their D8/D22 descendants only. Verified: production export shows 'Sel-' explainer goes from (EN/CL Seal) to (EN Seal) — false Celtic attribution gone. Regression test test_export_meanings_narrows_word_language_to_linked_etymons. 0 coverage regressions vs bundled meanings.json.

title: LLM disambiguator: group ambiguous rows by (source_id, matched_form) to dedupe LLM calls
description:
Follow-up to wyrd-6z7. find_ambiguous_rows currently returns one AmbiguityCase per etymon_text_match row, so when multiple fuzzy rows share the same (source_id, matched_form) — same body word, different originally-matched etymons — the disambiguator asks the LLM the same question multiple times.

Fix: group fuzzy rows by (source_id, matched_form) before constructing AmbiguityCase. Each case holds a list of text_match_ids to be updated/deleted together. apply_disambiguator_result becomes apply_disambiguator_result_for_group and writes the verdict to all rows in the group.

Acceptance: a regression test with two fuzzy rows for the same body word in the same source (different originally-matched etymons) results in one LLM call and a consistent verdict applied to both rows.

title: LLM disambiguator: agentic expand_context tool-call loop
description:
Follow-up to wyrd-6z7. The disambiguator currently uses a fixed snippet window. Per the wyrd-6z7 NOTES section, the model should be able to request more context when the initial snippet isn't sufficient.

Architecture: tool-call style with two tools: expand_context(direction, chars) and commit_answer(choice, confidence, reason). Orchestrator runs the conversation loop, capping at 3 expansion rounds or 2000 chars total.

Acceptance: a test case where the first 200 chars is genuinely ambiguous but the next 300 chars resolves it; disambiguator should request expansion and arrive at the correct answer.

title: [bug] Tier-2 review 'written' summary includes silently-dropped low-conf rows
description:
cli.py:1118-1120 increments counts['written'] for every accepted Gemini result, but ingest_parsed_entries in lexicon.py:1394 silently drops entries with confidence='low' (returns without inserting). Result: summary line claims more rows persisted than actually exist in DB.

Concrete example (2026-05-02): Ekwall 1922 Tier-2 review summary said 'written: 149', actual gemini rows in toponym_etymology for that source: 53. Discrepancy: 96 low-conf Gemini extractions silently dropped.

Fix options: (a) have ingest_parsed_entries return per-entry persistence status so cli.py can count accurately; (b) raise the writer's skip-low to a click.echo so it's visible; (c) check entry.confidence in cli.py before calling ingest_parsed_entries.

Not urgent — the silent drop is a sensible quality gate. Bug is in the *reporting*, not the data integrity. mining_run audit table reflects the inflated 'accepted' count too (D23), so any downstream stats should be aware.

title: Canonical-group rollup views for etymon_gloss, etymon_tag, etymon_text_match
description:
Why this exists:

After D22's non-destructive OCR clustering landed (wyrd-et0), glosses, tags, and text-match evidence stay attached to their original (loser) etymons rather than being moved to the canonical winner. The etymon_consensus view rolls up citations correctly via merged_into_id chains, but there is no equivalent rollup view for the other three child tables.

A direct SELECT against etymon_gloss / etymon_tag / etymon_text_match scoped to a canonical etymon's id will miss data attached to its merged tombstones. Compared to the previous destructive model where data was moved to the winner, this is a regression in 'what does this canonical etymon know?' visibility.

Flagged by Gemini in PR #7 review (https://github.com/521-studios/wyrd/pull/7).

What needs to be done:

Three new views, each unioning rows on the canonical-group rollup chain (the same COALESCE(merged_into_id, lemma_id, id) that etymon_consensus uses):

- etymon_gloss_canonical(canonical_etymon_id, gloss) DISTINCT
- etymon_tag_canonical(canonical_etymon_id, tag) DISTINCT
- etymon_text_match_canonical(canonical_etymon_id, source_id, matched_form, total_match_count, ...) — note the SUM aggregation for match_count parallels D21's UPSERT semantics

Audit existing direct queries against the underlying tables (the diagnostic SQL in INGESTION.md, the fuzzy-search EXISTS check in lexicon.py, any future report builders) and migrate them to read through the canonical views where the consumer wants 'all data for this canonical etymon, including from its merged variants.'

Acceptance:
- Three views created via migrate_schema (idempotent, recreated like etymon_consensus).
- Tests verify rollup correctness when an etymon has merged variants with their own glosses/tags/text-match rows.
- INGESTION.md's diagnostic queries updated to use the new views.
- No production code reads the underlying tables in a way that misses data attached to merged variants.

Soft prereq: wyrd-et0 (this PR).

title: Refactor cluster_ocr_variants: extract per-table merge logic
description:
Why this exists:

cluster_ocr_variants in wyrd/generators/kenning/lexicon.py is now ~120 lines after wyrd-go5's FK fix landed. The apply-phase loop (~76 lines) is a sequence of repetitive INSERT OR IGNORE / UPDATE / DELETE blocks, one per child table that references etymon. The repetition itself was the bug surface for wyrd-go5: when a new child table (etymon_text_match) was added, the merge loop wasn't updated and silently dropped rows.

Flagged by complexity-reviewer on PR #5 (https://github.com/521-studios/wyrd/pull/5).

What needs to be done:

Two viable shapes:
1. Extract a _merge_etymon_into(db, winner_id, loser_id) helper that owns the per-table merge sequence.
2. Build a declarative _ETYMON_CHILD_TABLES dispatch list — each entry names the child table, its UNIQUE-constraint columns, and any 'self-FK' column on etymon — and iterate it. Schema discoverability becomes auditable; future child tables get caught.

Acceptance:
- cluster_ocr_variants main body drops to fit one screen (~50 lines).
- All existing tests still pass; regression coverage from wyrd-go5 still exercises the new helper.
- Adding a hypothetical new child table requires updating one declarative list, not editing the merge loop body.

Likely supersedes interaction with wyrd-et0 — if non-destructive clustering lands, the merge loop becomes much shorter (mark-as-merged via merged_into_id), and this refactor is moot. Keep open as fallback if wyrd-et0 stalls.
close_reason: Obviated by wyrd-et0 (PR #7, commit 64a99c9). The non-destructive merge eliminates the per-table INSERT-OR-IGNORE/DELETE dispatch entirely — cluster_ocr_variants is now ~25 lines of merge logic with two UPDATEs (re-parent lemma children + mark merged_into_id with chain-flatten). No table-list refactor needed.

title: Batch SQL operations in cluster_ocr_variants
description:

Why deferred: cluster_ocr_variants runs occasionally during ingest, not in a hot path. Lexicon currently has ~few-hundred OCR variants tops; the chattiness hasn't caused observable slowdown. Worth doing as a focused optimization PR if/when it becomes a bottleneck.

title: server/SPA coerceToType integer divergence: server int() strict-rejects '5.0'/'3abc' where SPA parseInt is lenient (slider≠generation on malformed int default)
description:
Server/SPA coerceToType divergence on MALFORMED INTEGER input (pre-existing; surfaced by the PR #815 review, out of scope for that fix which only touched the non-finite number guard).

SPA spa-next/src/lib/featureFlags.js coerceToType (integer path): `parseInt(raw, 10)` — LENIENT, parses leading digits: parseInt('5.0',10)→5, parseInt('3abc',10)→3, parseInt('12px',10)→12.
Server wyrd/feature_flags.py _coerce_to_schema_type (integer path): `int(text)` — STRICT, rejects non-integer: int('5.0')→ValueError→None, int('3abc')→None.

So for an INTEGER option with a malformed default like WYRD_DEFAULT_COUNT=5.0 (a plausible operator input — writing an integer with a decimal point): the SPA seeds/displays 5 (parseInt), but the server's apply_env_defaults falls back to the SCHEMA default (int('5.0') rejected). Slider shows 5, generation uses the schema default → they DISAGREE (the wyrd-7f22 class). For clean integer strings ('5') both agree → 5. Only malformed integer input diverges.

Both behaviors are defensible (SPA lenient parseInt vs server strict int) but the docstring contract says the server "is the server-side mirror of the SPA's coerceToType" — so they should AGREE. FIX OPTIONS: (a) make the server emulate parseInt (parse leading integer digits — but that makes it LOOSER, accepting '3abc'→3, which is arguably worse); (b) make the SPA stricter (reject non-integer strings like the server) — cleaner, but a SPA behavior change; (c) for '5.0'-style (decimal-but-integral) specifically, server could int(float(text)) to match parseInt on those while still rejecting '3abc' (partial alignment). LOW priority — malformed-integer-default operator input only; clean inputs agree. Surfaced cycle-94.

title: runtime/word.py _bare_surface/_position_form de-dash ASCII-only (producer normalizes 11 dash codepoints) — latent pool-key fork, unreachable today
description:
runtime/word.py _bare_surface (L68) + _position_form (L80) de-dash with ASCII-only `.replace("-", "")` (strips U+002D only). The producer-side normalizer (lexicon/morpheme_surface.py normalize_morpheme_surface / _BOUNDARY_DASHES) strips 11 dash codepoints (U+2010 HYPHEN, U+2011 NBHY, en-dash U+2013, em-dash U+2014, U+2212 MINUS, …). So if a meaning.usage ever carries a NON-ASCII boundary/interior dash, word.py's strip leaves it in the proportions pool KEY — forking e.g. `Oak–` (en-dash) from the canonical `Oak`, silently splitting that morpheme's proportion weight across two keys.

UNREACHABLE on production today (confirmed cycle-92 audit): meaning.usage comes from the bundle's modern_usage, which is reconstructed by re-applying ASCII boundary dashes (`Great-`, `-great-`, `-great`) onto a canonical_form already de-dashed at upsert via normalize_morpheme_surface; validate_meanings.py enforces `"-" in modern_usage` (ASCII). So no unicode boundary dash reaches _bare_surface on real data. Probe: _bare_surface(Meaning("Oak–")) -> 'Oak–' (leaks), but no such usage is produced.

NOTE — interior ASCII hyphens are NOT this bug: 145/7111 toponym-breakdown morphemes (apple-tree, mill-stone, lēac-tūn) differ between `.replace("-","")` (strips interior → "appletree") and normalize (keeps interior → "apple-tree"). word.py DELIBERATELY strips ALL dashes for the runtime place-name SURFACE (its docstring: "dashes are NEVER part of it"), distinct from the lexicon's etymological IDENTITY which keeps the interior hyphen. The pool is built AND picked-from on the same stripped key → internally consistent. Do NOT "fix" by routing through normalize_morpheme_surface — that keeps interior hyphens and would wrongly change 145 runtime surfaces (appletree→apple-tree) + re-derive the pools. The correct hardening for THIS ticket is a unicode-AWARE strip-ALL (extend the stripped set to the 11 dash codepoints, keep the strip-all semantics) — byte-identical on current data (ASCII dashes stripped identically; no unicode dashes present), closing only the producer-vs-runtime alphabet asymmetry. Apply to BOTH _bare_surface and _position_form.

LOW priority — robustness gap, not a live bug (unreachable today). Surfaced by the cycle-92 runtime/word.py audit, which otherwise verified the module CLEAN (position-derivation lockstep _positioned_usages↔get_structure holds; lone/part pool routing edge case is matcher-unreachable; connective-collapse correct; __eq__/__hash__ consistent; saint-particle orthogonal; word_position_for no off-by-one).
notes: Cycle-93 reachability check (attempted the byte-identical fix, ABANDONED — not cleanly provable): 125 etymon canonical_forms DO carry a non-ASCII dash in storage (U+2011 NBHY on proto-roots like *bʰres‑, U+00AD soft-hyphen, en-dash in gloss-like 'Adolphe Sax (1814–1894)'), so a unicode-aware strip-ALL is NOT trivially byte-identical vs the current ASCII-only .replace — it differs on those 125. HOWEVER 0/125 appear in any toponym_etymology_element breakdown, and they are proto-roots / gloss forms, NOT promoted generation-bundle surface morphemes, so they don't reach _bare_surface via the runtime pool. So the fix is byte-identical on the breakdown-reachable data — BUT fully proving the matcher never free-decomposes a recorded toponym onto a non-ASCII-dash bundle morpheme needs more analysis than this P4 warrants. DEFER: do this de-dash-alphabet alignment as part of a deliberate proportions/priors pool rebuild (alongside wyrd-nkiq/ckro), where the pool is re-derived + diffed anyway, rather than forcing a "probably byte-identical" change to a load-bearing scoring primitive in an isolated PR. Keep P4.

title: runtime_db_export hardening: _bare_modern_usage strips ASCII-only (guard checks Unicode) + _write_meanings lacks sorted()
description:
A cycle-83 audit of runtime_db_export.py (the L4 publish boundary) closed the highest-value gap (PR #809: the D45 guard now scans blob language-form identity, not just modern_usage). Two LOWER-severity findings remain, neither a live bug:

1. _bare_modern_usage Unicode-dash scope mismatch (LOW, fails SAFE). _bare_modern_usage (lines ~159-167) de-dashes with value.replace("-", "") — ASCII hyphen U+002D ONLY (and the same ASCII-only fold at every write site: _iter_usage_rows, _iter_single_usage_rows, _insert_attested_languages, select_dev_subset; it mirrors runtime/word.py _bare_surface). But _verify_no_dashed_identity / _count_dashed_blob_identity use _BOUNDARY_DASHES (Unicode-aware: en-dash, em-dash, U+2010 HYPHEN, U+2011, minus sign, ...). So a modern_usage carrying a UNICODE boundary dash survives the de-dash unchanged, then trips the guard → the build RAISES instead of de-dashing it. Demonstrated: 'Oak–' (en-dash) → _bare_modern_usage keeps 'Oak–' → guard flags it. Fails SAFE (build fails loudly, no leak) and not reachable today (toponym.modern_name + reflex.surface_form have 0 Unicode-dashed rows). FIX: widen _bare_modern_usage to strip _BOUNDARY_DASHES at the boundary (like _strip_boundary_decoration), so the de-dash covers the SAME alphabet its own guard checks — and update runtime/word.py _bare_surface in lockstep (they must agree, since the runtime re-derives the bare key). Add a regression: a Unicode-dashed modern_usage de-dashes (not a build break).

2. _write_meanings lacks the defensive sorted() that _write_morphemes has (LOW, robustness asymmetry). _write_morphemes (~643) iterates `for morpheme_id in sorted(grouped)` for byte-stable row order independent of subject/word iteration order; _write_meanings (~600) iterates grouped.items() UNSORTED, so the meaning table's physical rowid order tracks upstream subject order. Not a live bug (the dev-seed drift test runs through select_dev_subset which sorts subjects via _subject_sort_key; the prod emit re-ships a fresh S3 key and isn't byte-compared; content is identical regardless of order). But it's an inconsistent reproducibility guarantee — the sibling writer guards the contract and this one relies on upstream. FIX: add `sorted(grouped)` (or sort by the same key as _write_morphemes) so the meaning emit is byte-stable independent of upstream order; confirm byte-identical on the current (already-sorted-upstream) emit.

Low priority — PR #809 closed the corrupting-risk gap (a dashed identity could SILENTLY ship). These two are a safe-direction build-breaker and a robustness asymmetry. Surfaced by the cycle-83 runtime_db_export.py audit.

title: merge_audit candidate-gen gaps: _affix_candidates is D45-inert (dead) + glossless-anchor dominant inference is a guess
description:
A cycle-82 audit of merge_audit.py verified the REVERT path correct (revert_rows un-merges the MEMBER not the anchor, provenance-routed to the right ledger/field, threshold-gated, idempotent; no D45 dash divergence; sense-clustering + determinism clean). But the candidate-GENERATION (the recall-oriented screen that feeds the LLM arbiter) has two gaps — neither corrupts the ledger, but both reduce which bad merges get audited/reverted:

1. _affix_candidates (Source: _is_affix at lines 81-85) is DEAD against the current corpus (HIGH confidence). _is_affix returns True only for a canonical_form starting/ending with a dash, but D40/D45 stores every form BARE: live ~/.wyrd/lexicon.db has 0 canonical_forms with a leading/trailing dash and 0 such with merged_into_id/lemma_id. So _affix_candidates yields ZERO candidates. The module's HEADLINE motivation (the docstring's -ton showing weight-unit 'ton', -ing's 45-gloss blob) is the exact class this source was built to catch — and it now can't, because the detector keys on a dash the de-dash invariant guarantees is absent. The -ton/-ing bad merges may still be caught by the disjoint-sense source (gloss-token split) — but that is UNMEASURED. DELIVERABLE: measure whether the disjoint-sense source actually catches the -ton/-ing-class OCR/lemma conflations (run detect_merge_audit_candidates on the live DB, check coverage of known bad merges); if yes, remove _is_affix/_affix_candidates as dead+redundant; if no, re-key the affix detector on a dash-independent signal (the POSITION axis / reflex position, since the canonical_form no longer carries the affix dash).

2. Glossless-anchor dominant-sense inference over-flags (MEDIUM, by-design, LLM-gated). In _anchor_intruders (~232) a glossless anchor is filtered out of `glossed`; with the anchor absent, `dominant` (~245) falls back to the largest MEMBER cluster — so the largest member sense is assumed correct with NO evidence the anchor matches it, and the other glossed members are flagged intruders. 97,690 canonical anchors are glossless and head families, so this is a high-volume guess. It over-flags (the LLM arbiter gates the actual revert, D21), so it doesn't corrupt — but it feeds the LLM lower-quality candidates for glossless anchors (the "dominant sense" is a coin-flip, not the anchor's sense). DELIVERABLE: when the anchor is glossless, either skip the disjoint-sense flag (no anchor evidence) or surface the ambiguity to the LLM (don't pre-pick a dominant), so the recall-oriented screen doesn't assert a guessed dominant.

Low priority — the revert path (the corrupting risk) is sound; these are recall/precision gaps in the screen. Surfaced by the cycle-82 merge_audit.py audit.

title: citations.py: Mawer header scraper mis-pages near all-caps body lines ending in an integer (data-quality hardening, pre-backfill)
description:
citations.py resolves a citation's page number by scraping OCR running headers (Mawer headword style "BACKWORTH 9" / Skeat section style). The Mawer parser (parse_running_header_pages) treats ANY all-caps line ending in an integer as a running header. A BODY line that happens to match that shape (e.g. "SEE ALSO 12", a cross-reference, or an all-caps entry name followed by a stray OCR integer) is parsed as a spurious header → injects a false page boundary → page_for_offset then mis-assigns the wrong page to quotes/citations near that offset until the next real header. This is the inherent limitation of header-pattern scraping (documented heuristic), NOT a code logic bug — page_for_offset, the offset convention, the regex captures, the tie-break, idempotency, and determinism were all verified correct (cycle-78 hunter).

SEVERITY: LOW + currently latent. The pages are DISPLAY-ONLY provenance (bundle/browse.py + jsonl/dump.py render p.page; they do NOT feed any game_id — there is no game_id machinery in the kenning lexicon). And backfill-citation-pages is UNRUN on the live DB (all 34,363 etymon_citation + 19,921 toponym_etymology pages are NULL), so no wrong page is committed yet — the risk materializes only when an operator runs the backfill.

HARDENING (if pursued): add a header/body discriminator before treating an all-caps+integer line as a running header — e.g. require the page integers to be monotonic-ish across the doc, require the headword to match a known toponym/headword, or require the line to sit at a physical page top (form-feed / blank-line context). Validate against the source OCR before running backfill. Also a minor coverage gap (not wrong-page): Skeat "§8.NAMES" with NO space after the period yields no match (the regex requires \s+ after the period) — reduces Skeat header yield, never assigns a wrong page. Low priority.

title: fold_surface drops Old Norse stroke-letters (o-slash/o-ogonek/l-stroke) mid-word instead of folding to base
description:
genitive_priors.fold_surface (the system-wide D45 surface fold) expands the OE ligatures ae/oe/th/d via _LIGATURES then NFKD then encode(ascii, ignore). NFKD decomposes accented letters (a-ring to a) but does NOT decompose STROKE letters (o-slash/O-slash, o-ogonek, l-stroke, d-stroke - the stroke is not a combining mark), so encode(ascii, ignore) DROPS them mid-word: Sonderby (with o-slash) folds to snderby (loses the o-slash), inconsistent with AElfric folding to aelfric. Old Norse uses o-slash/o-ogonek, and the generator handles Norse cognates, so such a form folds to a partial surface that will not match its o-spelling - a RECALL gap in fold-based surface grouping (same_morpheme_mining by_surface, decomposition_grader surface_clusters). NOT corruption: empty/partial folds are guarded (if not folded continue) and do not collide/wrong-merge (D46 missed-merge-harmless).

NOTE the tens-of-thousands of Greek/Arabic surfaces in the corpus fold to empty and are correctly EXCLUDED (guarded) - by-design for an English generator, not a bug; this ticket is ONLY about the Latin-script stroke-letters that partial-fold.

FIX (if pursued): add the stroke letters (o-slash to o, o-ogonek to o, l-stroke to l, d-stroke to d) to _LIGATURES, plus audit other non-decomposing Latin letters. CAUTION: this is a SYSTEM-WIDE identity-fold change - it re-groups every stroke-letter-bearing surface everywhere fold_surface is used, re-positioning committed surface_clusters / bundle / same-morpheme data (cycle-68/wyrd-qdau class). Measure the blast-radius against the live DB BEFORE changing, and treat as a coordinated code+data step, not a code-only PR. Low priority: harmless recall gap, possibly-intended OE calibration. Surfaced by a cycle-74 bug-hunter sweep of genitive_priors.py (the module itself verified clean).

title: Phase 4 (worldbuild): cultural geography — language families, religion, kinship over the economic-geographic substrate
description:
The integration layer. Takes geology + climate + economics output and produces realistic cultural-geographic distribution: language-family migration patterns, religious-syncretism zones, kinship-system distributions, food cultures, material-culture vocabularies.

This is the layer that ties everything BACK to onomastics. When the onomastics layer asks 'what's the Brittonic-substrate weight for this region?' or 'how strong is Norman influence here?', this layer answers — and answers REPRODUCIBLY based on the geology + climate + economic-history that produced the linguistic substrate distribution.

DELIBERATE QUALITY BAR: 'defensible enough to publish.' Use existing historical-linguistics + anthropology of kinship frameworks; don't try to advance those subfields. Publishable contribution is the integration architecture (cultural geography emerges from the underlying economic-geographic substrate + history; downstream-consumable for onomastics).

INPUT (from Phase 3 + the broader stack):
- Settlement-graph + trade-network + economic-history
- Geology (mountain barriers, river highways)
- Climate (which biomes support which subsistence strategies)
- World parameters: starting cultural-linguistic seeds, time depth, migration-event triggers

OUTPUT (consumable by onomastics — wyrd-kz2b stack):
- Language-family distribution per region per era
- Substrate / superstrate layer metadata per region (e.g. 'Brittonic substrate + Anglo-Saxon superstrate + Norman superstrate' for southeast English placenames)
- Religious distribution + syncretism zones
- Kinship-system distribution
- Food-culture metadata (what's eaten, what's named after food)
- Material-culture vocabulary domains
- Process trace per region (when language X arrived, when religion Y converted, etc.)

SCHOLARSHIP TRACE:
- Cite historical-linguistics (Renfrew 'Archaeology and Language', Anthony 'The Horse, the Wheel, and Language', Garrett on PIE homeland)
- Cite anthropology-of-kinship (Murdock Ethnographic Atlas, more recent quantitative work)
- Cite religious-syncretism studies
- Cite genetic + linguistic phylogenetics (Bouckaert et al. 2012 Indo-European Bayesian phylogeography)
- Cite Diamond 'Guns Germs and Steel' (cited critically + with appropriate caveats)

EXISTING WORK TO BUILD ON:
- D-PLACE (Database of Places, Language, Culture, Environment) — already an integrated cross-cultural database; methodology can borrow extensively
- Glottolog (language family classification)

PUBLICATION OUTPUT:
- Code repository
- Methodology paper (target: a historical-linguistics-meets-CS venue OR a cross-disciplinary digital-humanities venue like JOHD)
- Reference dataset of generated cultural geographies

DEPENDS ON: Phases 1-3 landing. Closes the loop with wyrd-kz2b onomastics.

THE NAME-FOR-THIS-LAYER QUESTION: 'cultural geography' is the working name; 'historical-linguistic-substrate-distribution' is the more technical name. The manifesto paper (wyrd-x8r2 child) will need to land on terminology.

title: MCP-enriched mine-llm for agentic etymology decomposition via lexicon DB
description:
Exploration ticket for letting the etymology-decomposition LLM query the wyrd lexicon DB on-demand during inference via Model Context Protocol (MCP), rather than (or in addition to) static RAG prompt enrichment proposed in wyrd-gz66.

The shape: stand up an MCP server exposing read-only lexicon tools to the LLM, so during decomposition of a dictionary entry the LLM can iterate: query → reason → query again → propose decomposition → verify against DB → finalize. This is the 'agentic loop' pattern, distinct from one-shot RAG.

MCP server tool surface (read-only, ~4-6 tools):
- lookup_briggs(toponym) -> {pn_headform, pn_language, attested_form_variants, county}
- match_mawer_element(suffix_or_form) -> [{element, language, gloss, semantic_category}]
- find_similar_toponyms(form, suffix=None) -> [toponym_decomposition]
- get_canonical_decomposition(toponym) -> {elements, consensus_size, source_extractors}
- verify_pn_attestation(pn_headform) -> {is_attested: bool, source, period}
- (optional) search_attested_forms(form_pattern) -> matching attestations

Pre-flight smoke test required BEFORE any architecture commitment:

The local-ollama path is only viable if gemma4:26b (or successor model on our macbook) can do multi-step tool-use reliably. Run a 10-entry smoke test with a simple tool schema (lookup + match + final_answer) on a wyrd-flavored task. Measure:
- Tool-call rate: does the model actually USE the tools or ignore them?
- Multi-step capability: does it iterate (call → use result → call again → stop)?
- Stop reliability: does it terminate with a final answer or loop indefinitely?

Decision matrix from smoke test:
- ≥60% reliable multi-step → local-tier MCP viable (cheap, agentic-on-macbook)
- 30-60% → cloud-tier (haiku/gemini-flash) only, where tool-use is reliable
- <30% → consider holding off; the RAG approach (wyrd-gz66) probably captures most of the value with none of the operational complexity

Architecture options based on smoke test outcome:

PATH A (local-tier capable):
- ollama gemma4 or qwen3 or successor with native tool-use
- MCP server on the same host (low-latency)
- ~3-5× per-entry wall-clock vs prompt-only, but on free local compute
- Slots into cascade as a new Tier 1 'agentic' mode alongside the existing bulk Tier 1

PATH B (cloud-tier only):
- haiku-4.5 or gemini-2.5-flash with tool-use
- MCP server runs locally; cloud LLM calls into it via the MCP bridge
- ~3-5× per-call cost on the cascade-stage-3 tier
- Reserved for the residual hard cases that prompt-only mine-llm couldn't decompose at high confidence

Implementation surface for either path:

1. MCP server: stand up an MCP server (likely Python — Anthropic provides a Python SDK) exposing the 4-6 tools above. Use the existing lexicon.py module for DB access. Read-only, no write capabilities.

2. Aggressive caching: many queries will be repeats ('is -hām a real element?' / 'lookup Ælfric'). LRU cache the tool implementations.

3. Cost guards / loop limits: per-decomposition, cap at N tool calls (e.g. 8) and N total LLM round-trips (e.g. 5). Fall back to RAG-only on cap exhaustion.

4. mine-llm integration: optional --use-mcp flag on the existing mine-llm command. When enabled, the etymology extractor talks to the LLM via MCP-aware client code (handles the agentic loop). When disabled, uses prompt-only with wyrd-gz66 RAG context.

5. A/B harness: rerun a fixed sample set with --use-mcp on vs off, compare extraction quality (PN agreement with Briggs, element-position correctness, language-tag correctness). Measure quality lift vs cost multiplier.

Sequencing (this ticket is far in the future):
- Prerequisite: wyrd-uzoh (Briggs in DB) — without this the MCP server has nothing useful to expose
- Strongly recommended precursor: wyrd-gz66 (RAG prompt enrichment) — if RAG gets us to ≥95%% precision, the marginal value of MCP-agentic over RAG might not justify its complexity. Measure first.
- Also benefits from: wyrd-1zx9 (deterministic decomposer) being shipped first, so the Briggs-covered subset is removed from the LLM pipeline entirely before we invest in agentic LLM tooling for the residual

Pairs naturally with:
- wyrd-e67 (Bedrock provider for runtime LLM features) — the MCP server is independently useful for runtime/GM-facing features
- wyrd-sreb (narrative-driven scenario translation) — that work is inherently agentic (LLM picks scenario-pack subsets based on narrative) and would benefit from the same MCP infrastructure if we build it

Out of scope:
- Building MCP servers for non-lexicon data (separate ticket if pursued)
- Write-capable MCP tools (out of scope for this exploration — risk too high)
- Cloud-tier MCP without first measuring the local-tier viability

The user's framing at file time: 'we're no where near doing this right now' — this is an architectural option captured for future consideration after wyrd-uzoh + wyrd-gz66 land and we measure the RAG-only baseline.
notes:
2026-05-18 update: candidate model added — Google FunctionGemma (Dec 2025).

FunctionGemma is Google's specialist function-calling model built on Gemma 3 270M (270M params). Purpose-built for the agentic-loop pattern described in this ticket. Available on ollama as 'functiongemma' (ollama.com/library/functiongemma) and on HuggingFace as google/functiongemma-270m-it.

Key data points from Google's own published evaluation:
- Mobile Actions benchmark: 58%% zero-shot accuracy, 85%% after task-specific fine-tuning
- 270M params means it runs anywhere — no VRAM contention with the gemma4:26b mining run
- Designed as "intelligent traffic controller for larger connected systems" per Google's docs — explicitly architected for the small-orchestrator + big-reasoner pattern

The 58%% zero-shot number is sobering. Out-of-the-box, FunctionGemma will mis-orchestrate ~4 in 10 calls on Google's own benchmark. For production-grade agentic decomposition we'd need fine-tuning on wyrd-flavored examples, which requires a training corpus of (entry → correct tool-call sequence → correct decomposition) triples — a separate data-prep problem we don't have data for yet.

Architecture implication: two-model deployment becomes the preferred shape, not single-model.

PATH C (added as the FunctionGemma option):
- FunctionGemma (270M) handles agentic-loop orchestration: decides which MCP tool to call, processes results, decides next call, terminates with synthesis hand-off
- gemma4:26b OR haiku/gemini-flash handles the final synthesis (the actual etymology decomposition) once FunctionGemma has gathered context
- This splits the 'agentic-loop' concern (small specialist, FunctionGemma) from the 'reasoning' concern (big general model)
- Latency-friendly: FunctionGemma runs on CPU/lightweight GPU; the synthesizer runs once at the end
- Cost-friendly if synthesizer is local; reasonable if cloud (only one cloud-tier call per decomposition, not 3-5)

Smoke test scope expanded:
- Configuration A: single-model agentic with gemma4:26b (original test)
- Configuration B: single-model agentic with qwen3:32b (stronger local agentic baseline)
- Configuration C: two-model FunctionGemma orchestrator + gemma4:26b synthesizer
- Configuration D: two-model FunctionGemma orchestrator + haiku synthesizer

Measure per-config: tool-call accuracy (does it call the right tool at the right time?), loop termination rate (does it stop cleanly?), final decomposition correctness (against the wyrd-1zx9 deterministic ground truth for Briggs-covered toponyms).

Pick the lowest-cost configuration with ≥85%% reliability. Fine-tune FunctionGemma later if Path C/D show promise but need accuracy lift.

Sources:
- https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/functiongemma/
- https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/capabilities/function-calling
- https://ollama.com/library/functiongemma
- https://huggingface.co/google/functiongemma-270m-it

title: Scenario-pack: counterfactual Tatar-invades-England pilot (validates Option B generalization)
description:
Counterfactual-history scenario pack. Tatar/Mongol/Turkic lemmas templated via Mongol->Russian adaptation patterns (wyrd-8a5r) RE-TARGETED to OE-era English phonotactic constraints.

Validates the Option B generalization claim: empirical-baseline data from one loan relationship (Mongol->Russian) extrapolates cleanly to a counterfactual recipient (Mongol->OE-English) via the adaptation engine.

Composes with the user's stated long-term vision: 'area raided by horsemen, great, we'll add mongol loan words' — the narrative-translator (wyrd-sreb) eventually selects this pack subset automatically when narrative matches.

Dependencies:

Demonstrates that 'fantasy', 'counterfactual', and 'speculative' are mechanically identical from the architecture's perspective.

title: EPIC: wholly-new constructed languages (phonaesthetic-vector composition)
description:
Generate a wholly new fantasy language from a user-supplied phonaesthetic vector + flavor weights. No real-language names in the user-facing palette; only register-effect axes (harsh, noble, mystical, martial, ancient, melodic, sinister, exotic, ...). Per [[phonaesthetic-vector-design-refinement-2026-05-16-user]].

Operator workflow:
1. Declare vector: {harsh: 0.5, mystical: 0.3, ancient: 0.2}
2. System composes phonological feature spec from register-effect-to-feature mappings (calibrated against phonaesthetics literature + LLM-graded audit)
3. Lemma generator produces N phonotactically-coherent candidates
4. Tag-assignment LLM loop pairs lemmas with semantic glosses at operator-declared tag distribution
5. Inflection-paradigm starter templates per inflection-style choice (agglutinative / fusional / isolating)
6. Era-progression: each lemma walks back through 3-4 eras via inverse sound-change rules (composes with D33 era-reflex + KenningRewind)

Sub-phases (rough):
1. Phonaesthetic vector schema + register-effect catalog
2. Register-effect-to-phonological-feature mapping table (literature-grounded; LLM-audited)
3. Lemma generator (phonotactic-grammar sampling under constraints)
4. Tag-assignment LLM loop
5. Inflection-paradigm starter templates
6. Inverse sound-change rules + backward era projection (modern -> middle -> old -> ancient)
7. Pack-build integration
8. Documentation: honest framing that phonaesthetic mappings are calibrated to English-speaker audience perception (the SHIPPED-AUDIENCE), not linguistic-universal truth; real-language inventories used only as internal research input

Estimated 5-6 weeks. Composes with derived-langs epic; reuses adaptation runtime infrastructure from wyrd-v2gm Phase 3.

title: EPIC: derived-language packs (Drow-from-Quenya pattern; delta-vector driven)
description:
Daughter-language pack generation: take a parent fantasy/real pack and derive a child pack via a single phonaesthetic delta vector. Drow-from-Quenya is the canonical example — operator declares 'Drow is Quenya with -0.7 noble, +0.5 harsh, +0.6 sinister, +0.4 martial'; system derives the rest.

Core insight (per phonaesthetic-vector design refinement, [[phonaesthetic-vector-design-refinement-2026-05-16-user]]): a daughter language = parent_vector + delta_vector. Sound-change rules, semantic-tag shift, and lexical retention all fall out of the delta vector direction. No hand-curated rule chains required.

Sub-phases (rough):
1. Delta-vector schema + parent-pack reference mechanism
2. Sound-change rule derivation from vector direction (auto-derive: amplifying harsh => insert cluster-fortition rules; suppressing noble => suppress vowel-final-bias rules; etc.)
3. Semantic-tag shift derivation (auto-derive: lower noble => suppress noble-coded glosses; raise sinister => amplify sinister-coded glosses)
4. Lexical retention algorithm (parent lemmas survive in proportion to their tag's vector alignment in the daughter)
5. Operator review tool (preview daughter pack vs parent; tweak delta and re-render)
6. Drow-from-Quenya pilot

Estimated 1.5-2 weeks; most schema/algorithm work; reuses adaptation runtime + tag system.

Composes with wholly-new-langs epic (same phonaesthetic-vector primitive). Demonstrates the architecture generalizes from loan-adaptation -> daughter-language with no new aesthetic-input mechanism.

title: Scenario-pack: Klingon — ON template (with caveats; proves sci-fi scope)
description:
Marc Okrand's Klingon (~3,500-word published lexicon, tlhIngan Hol). Distinctive uvular + glottal stop phonology has no clean real-language donor match.

Best fit: Old Norse template (percussive consonants, monosyllabic-leaning, martial register). Caveats:
- Klingon's /Q/ uvular stop + /'/ glottal don't map cleanly to ON phonemes; adaptation rules will need creative substitution (Q -> kh? cluster? OE didn't have /Q/ either)
- Klingon retroflex /D/ similarly orphaned
- Reach: would prove the epic works for sci-fi register, not just fantasy

Pilot dependency: Phase 6. Effectively shares Neo-Khuzdul's ON empirical base — extra template work is the Klingon-specific phoneme-map fork, not new corpus mining.

title: Scenario-pack: Adûnaic — Akkadian/Semitic template (architecturally novel)
description:
Tolkien's Númenórean lang (Lowdham's Report; Sauron Defeated). Semitic root-and-pattern morphology gives it a genuinely distinct sound vs. the OE/ME-substrate-flavored Khuzdul/Sindarin/Quenya packs.

Composes uniquely with the existing wyrd-ami approved-languages list (D30): hebrew, akkadian, aramaic, egyptian ISO codes are already in APPROVED_LANGUAGES.

Best loan template: Akkadian -> Old English (hypothetical historical contact via Mediterranean trade routes) OR Akkadian -> Modern English (scholarly Orientalist register, post-Layard).

Dependency: real-world Akkadian/Semitic -> English adaptation profile must exist as a template source (separate infrastructure ticket).

Architecturally important: this is the pack that proves the epic isn't OE/Celtic-substrate-limited — it can handle a fully non-Indo-European donor.

title: Scenario-pack: High Valyrian — Latin-template-EModE (classical language of Essos)

High Valyrian as the 'Latin of Essos' — ceremonial/classical/imperial register. Latin->EModE template (post-Renaissance scholarly revival shape) vs OE-era Latin (Roman castra layer).

Caveat: latin->old-english EModE has only 4 element appearances (very thin). Likely need to augment by also walking Latin->ModE (modern scholarly loans like 'aqueduct', 'imperium', 'senate') as the calibration set.

The 'High Valyrian as Renaissance-revival Latin' framing may also be cleaner via Latin->ModE-with-classical-stylings than EModE proper.

title: Scenario-pack: Quenya — Latin template (OE-era, high-register liturgical)
description:
Quenya as 'the Latin of Middle-earth' — high-register ecclesiastical/scholarly. Maps onto Latin->OE profile (492 element appearances, OE-era dominant at 222 attestations).

title: Scenario-pack: Sindarin — Celtic template (ME-era best fit)
description:
Second fantasy-language pack after Neo-Khuzdul pilot lands. Sindarin's elf-aesthetic vector (water, forest, song, melancholy) maps onto Celtic-substrate -> OE/ME profile:
- Celtic donor data is richest in the corpus (3,514 element appearances)
- Topography-heavy (12% of Celtic toponym contributions vs OE 10%)
- Initial-position-leaning (40% initial)
- Tolkien internal-lore lines up: Sindarin is the 'speech of the woods' similar to Brythonic substrate role

ME-era ingest probably the best fit; Tolkien's framing of 'Westron-with-Elvish-loans' is post-Conquest-shaped.

Pilot dependency: Phase 6 must complete; this pack reuses the same epic infrastructure.

title: Add provider attribution (notes_prefix) to source_quote on the decline path
description:
Per Gemini review on PR #28: when an LLM extractor returns found=False, the assemble_extraction_result decline path stores body[:SOURCE_QUOTE_BUDGET] WITHOUT the notes_prefix attribution. The accepted path includes 'extracted_by:<provider>:<model>' as a prefix; the decline path doesn't. This makes it impossible to distinguish 'Gemini declined this entry' from 'Qwen declined' from 'baseline regex produced no body' when querying the lexicon later.

Current behavior (intentional per the existing test docstring):
  source_quote = body[:SOURCE_QUOTE_BUDGET]

Proposed:
  source_quote = (notes_prefix + ' | ' + body)[:SOURCE_QUOTE_BUDGET]

Trade-off:
- Pro: per-provider attribution on declines enables 'show me all toponyms Gemini Flash declined' queries; helps identify which model is over-declining a given content shape.
- Con: small loss of body context (~30-50 chars consumed by the prefix). The SPA citation view doesn't render decline rows in the same way as accepted rows anyway.
- Con: changes the documented contract on test_assemble_extraction_result_not_found_emits_low_confidence_entry. Update the test + docstring to match.

This is OUT OF SCOPE for PR #28 (which is about budget, not attribution). Filed separately so it's not lost.

See PR #28 comment 3177442609.
close_reason: landed in PR #34 (wyrd-9v1, skeat_parser budget alignment) + PR #35 (wyrd-6hd, decline-path provider attribution). Both merged 2026-05-03.

title: MCP server: expose wyrd APIs to GMs via Claude / other AI assistants
description:
Wrap the wyrd HTTP API (or core generation functions directly) as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server so GMs can use Claude / Cursor / other AI assistants to call the generator with rich natural-language constraints.

Use case: GM says to Claude 'give me 10 names for villages in a Norse-influenced coastal region in the 12th century, all with water-related morphemes, presented as a markdown table with pronunciation guides.' Claude calls wyrd's MCP tools to actually generate, then formats as requested.

Tools to expose:
- generate(culture, era, register, tags, count, novelty, seed) → list of structured names with breakdowns
- explain(name) → morpheme decomposition with all matching readings
- convert(name, target_register) → cross-register rendering (when wyrd-4cd ships)
- pronounce(name, language) → respelling + IPA
- lexicon_search(form_or_gloss) → all etymons matching, with citations
- list_pantheons() / get_deity(pantheon, name) → for deity-based naming
- pin_name(name, target_register) → conjugate user-supplied name into register

Architecture options:
1. Python MCP server using the official Python SDK, calls into wyrd's existing generate/explain functions directly (no HTTP). Cleanest for a single-machine GM.
2. HTTP-fronting MCP server that calls the deployed lambda. Useful for multi-user setups.
3. Both (start with 1, add 2 if there's demand).

Distribution: package as 'wyrd-mcp' with an entry point in pyproject.toml, then a GM does:
  pip install wyrd-mcp
  # add to ~/.config/Claude/mcp_servers.json
  # restart Claude
  # GM types: 'generate me 5 elven villages in the Shire'

Killer feature: GM gets fluent natural-language access to a constrained, reproducible generator — Claude handles the parsing of intent, wyrd handles the constrained generation. Better than either alone.

value: generator-composition-pattern-multi-result-false-loop: When composing one Generator inside another (e.g. KenningEraMap calling Kenning), drive the inner loop manually with seed+i offsets. Reason: Kenning is multi_result=False, so the framework dispatcher does the count-loop externally — calling kenning.generate(params, seed) returns ONE name, not a list. Inside another generator's generate_all, you must loop seed+i yourself OR call kenning.generate_all(params, seed) which inherits the default single-result wrap. See PR #129 KenningEraMap for the canonical pattern: dedupe by tracked-set, skip on collision.

waiter-loop-self-reference-bug: When using `until ! pgrep -f "<pattern>"; do sleep 30; done; tail ...` as a background-task waiter, the pgrep itself matches the parent shell's argv (which contains the pattern literally as a string). The until loop then never exits. Three waiters in 2026-05-04/05 spun for 10-12 hours each before the user noticed in the UI. Fix: check by PID instead — capture the target PID first via `P=$(pgrep -f '<pattern>' | head -1)`, then `until ! kill -0 $P 2>/dev/null; do sleep 30; done`. Or just use `run_in_background: true` on the actual command and trust the task-notification system to fire when it exits — don't write waiter loops at all.

worktree-isolation-from-side-branch-pr-96: Confirmed PR #96 (2026-05-07) that the cwd-import-priority trick works for running worktree-edited code against the live ~/.wyrd/lexicon.db without modifying the main repo's source tree. From the worktree directory, 'python -c "sys.argv = [...]; from wyrd.cli import main; main()"' wins over the editable install because Python's cwd-prepend on sys.path runs before site-packages lookup. pr-review-loop agent reviewers can run 'git checkout' inside the shared worktree and hijack its branch — on PR #542 a complexity agent checked out a 'pr-542' branch, so the next commit-and-push.sh landed the review fix on pr-542 instead of the PR's real branch (PR head silently stayed at the pre-fix commit). MITIGATION: (1) tell every review agent 'do NOT switch git branches or create any branch' in its prompt; (2) after agents run, before commit-and-push, verify 'git branch --show-current' matches the PR branch. RECOVERY: git checkout <pr-branch>; git merge --ff-only <stray>; git push origin <pr-branch>; git branch -D <stray>; git push origin --delete <stray>.

When user has multiple Claude sessions running in parallel on the same canonical lexicon DB, work can collide. Concrete example 2026-05-03: I (Claude 2) made plus-variant template extensions to wiktextract_ingester.py while another session simultaneously merged PR #44 and made the IDENTICAL changes (commit f1cd0e2 on main). My changes ended up redundant. Mitigation: at session start, after /clear, run 'git fetch origin && git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD' AND 'git log origin/main -5' to spot recent main advances. Also check git status for unexpected branch switches — the gitStatus from session start can be stale if another session checked out a different branch in the same worktree.

promotion-thresholds-per-language: D4's '≥3 witnesses' promotion threshold is per-language, not a global constant. Reason: many languages (Welsh, Irish, Breton, Old Welsh, Old Norse, etc.) have far fewer source materials than English; a flat ≥3 effectively excludes them. Each language carries its own threshold tuned to its corpus depth. Per user 2026-05-08 in the gap-closing-epic context. How to apply: every promotion-eligibility query / dashboard metric / mining-decision must read the per-language threshold (lexicon-side config, NOT a hardcoded 3). For language-quality dashboard (wyrd-wzwa) this means metric A's 'promotion-eligible' count uses the language's threshold, AND the dashboard should surface the threshold itself as an input row (so 'promotion-eligible: 14/97 [threshold=2]' is more legible than '14/97'). Look at where the existing ≥3 default lives in the lexicon code and treat it as the english-default when no per-language override is present.

When an agent (Explore, Task, etc.) summarizes mining stats, model performance, or any quantitative claim about the lexicon corpus — OR makes a content-shape verdict on a mining-source candidate (e.g. 'this is essay-shaped / low yield', 'this is a dictionary, will mine well') — ALWAYS verify against actual data before propagating to docs or decisions.

Five documented instances now (and counting):

1. 2026-05-01: a transcript-mining agent reported 'Watson 1904 Haiku 6× yield over Qwen' — actual mining_run data showed Haiku 3% vs Qwen 7% on Watson 1904 (both poor — Watson 1926 is the Haiku-earns-it case at 52%).

2. 2026-05-02: a probe agent verdict on Quilgars 1906 was based on raw OCR keyword counts (dense Plou-/Ker- prefix presence) rather than body content. Reality: 3% accept rate because Quilgars is a topographical (property-record) dictionary, not toponymic etymology.

3. 2026-05-02: prior session called Longnon 1920 and Loth 1890 'essay-shaped, low parser yield' from titles + surface signals. Re-probe found Longnon vol 1 yields 67 parser entries × 24% accept = 16 acc / 27 etymons; Loth 1890 is actually a Middle Breton text anthology where the etymology commentary is a small fraction of bulk. Both initial 'low yield' calls were wrong about the REASON; final yields ended up modest because of structural mismatches the original framing missed.

4. 2026-05-03: Joret 1881 Bessin smoke. Title 'Essai sur le patois Normand du Bessin; suivi d'un dictionnaire étymologique' suggested toponymic etymology but the dictionary section is NORMAN DIALECT WORDS + Latin etymons (Etande ← extendere, Foche ← focacia), not toponymic. Pipeline-mismatched.

5. 2026-05-03: d'Arbois 1890 yield projection. Initial smoke showed 40% accept on first 30 entries; full pass dropped to 10% as later chapters got more abstract. Lesson: smoke-the-FIRST-N is biased because front-matter / dense early chapters / sparse tail aren't uniformly distributed across a 700-page treatise. ALSO: the 800-floor on the attested_year validator (set conservatively for British Norman-period sources) cut 39 legitimate Roman-era citations on this source — fixed via wyrd-z56 widening to 100, recovered 27 rows on re-mine.

Why: agents synthesize from indirect sources; the DB / actual OCR body is the ground truth. Yield projections from prose-density samples consistently diverge from parser-yield at mining time. Validators' default ranges may be miscalibrated for source classes outside their original design context.

How to apply:
- For source-candidate probes: pull the IA *_djvu.txt URL; sample 3-5 contiguous ~500-word excerpts from spaced positions; count named places + explicit etymological links per passage; CONFIRM the parser yield (run _select_parser_and_run); only THEN smoke 30-50 entries via LLM. The parser-yield step is the one most often skipped and most-likely to surprise.
- For corpus-stats claims: run the equivalent SQL against mining_run / toponym_etymology and reconcile; flag and fix any divergence in the agent's prose before using it.
- For VALIDATOR rejection patterns: when rejection counts are dominated by a specific rule (e.g. attested_year_out_of_range), check whether the source class differs from the validator's design context; widening / per-source overrides may recover real data.

Architectural decisions: D1 multi-axis vector model (phonological/semantic/position/empirical-baseline); D2 baseline is just one axis with continuous weight, not a separate 'realism' concept (auto-blend with register effects; pack-weight is INDEPENDENT); D3 OPTION B for pack-lemma baselines — pack lemmas inherit their template's empirical loan-relationship baseline (Khuzdul pack templated on ON->OE uses wyrd-o3rh ON->OE baseline mining as its reference; 'bare --culture english --pack neo-khuzdul' produces historically-shaped output where Khuzdul appears at the rate real Norse loans appeared); D4 D17 cohesion preserved via adapter; D5 culture is hard gate v1; D6 --tag stays per user direction; D7 per (culture × position × tag × era) granularity; D8 tolerance bands deferred to Phase 6a empirical drift measurement. Pack-weight scales the pack baseline. Phonaesthetic-vector design refinement (2026-05-16, user-clarified): the universal aesthetic primitive across the fantasy-language epic family is a vector of REGISTER EFFECTS (harsh, noble, mystical, martial, ancient, melodic, sinister, exotic, ...) — NOT real-language names. Each register effect maps to PHONOLOGICAL FEATURE CORRELATES (cluster density, final-position bias, consonant softness, vowel-final rate, etc.). Real-language phonological inventories serve as INTERNAL RESEARCH INPUT for calibrating which features produce which effects, never appear in the user-facing palette. Grounded in phonaesthetics + sound-symbolism literature (Hinton/Nichols/Ohala 1994 'Sound Symbolism'; Köhler bouba/kiki; Ohala frequency code; Whissell's phonemic-emotion studies). Architectural payoff: phonaesthetic vectors are the universal aesthetic primitive across (1) loan-adaptation packs [wyrd-v2gm epic], (2) derived-language packs [Drow-from-Quenya = parent_vector + delta_vector], (3) wholly-new-language packs [new_vector composed from register-effect weights]. For derived-langs: operator supplies just the delta vector; sound-change rules, semantic-tag shift, and lexical retention all fall out of the vector direction. No hand-curated rule chains. Cleans up the cultural-baggage problem of the prior 'flavor = real-language' design ([[cultural-sensitivity-policy-refinement-2026-05-16-user]]). See [[fantasy-language-town-name-generation-epic-wyrd-v2gm]].

CI installs ruff unpinned (pip install -e .[dev], ruff>=0.4), so it resolves to the LATEST ruff at run time. A stale local ruff format-flags files that CI's newer ruff accepts (hit this on PR #681: local 0.14.13 flagged a blank-line in an unrelated file; CI used 0.15.18 and was green). Before trusting a local 'ruff format --check' diff on a file you didn't touch, pin local ruff to CI's version: read it from a recent green main CI run via 'gh run view <id> --log | grep -o ruff-[0-9.]*', then 'pip install ruff==<that>'. Otherwise you chase phantom format diffs or, worse, reformat to a shape CI then rejects.

SQLite LIKE on a BLOB column silently matches ZERO rows. The L4 runtime DB stores JSON blobs as bytes (.encode('utf-8')) in BLOB columns → storage class 'blob'. A 'WHERE blob_col LIKE ...' with a TEXT pattern NEVER matches → the query returns nothing regardless of content. This silently neutered the D45 dash-guard's blob check (wyrd-aicu.5, PR #630, caught in round-3 review). Two fixes: CAST(data AS TEXT) LIKE works, OR prefilter in Python on the fetched value (b'-' in data — robust, no storage-class trap). Also: tests must insert blobs as BYTES (json.dumps(...).encode()), not str — a str insert lands as TEXT storage class where LIKE works, giving false-green for any storage-class-sensitive bug.
